why: Ask a class how they revise and most of them will describe some version of reading their notes again. It's completely understandable, because re-reading feels productive while you're doing it. The trouble is that the feeling is misleading. Reading something again mostly gives pupils a sense of familiarity with the page, and familiarity isn't the same thing as being able to remember the material when they need it.

Roediger and Karpicke showed this really clearly. Students who were tested on material remembered far more of it weeks later than students who spent the same amount of time re-reading it. The card puts the implication plainly: the testing is the learning, not the preparation for it.
example: Before an end-of-topic check, an English class spends ten minutes writing down what they can remember about a poem's imagery, with their anthology notes closed. Then they open the notes and check what they've written against them. It takes the same amount of time as a read-through would have done, but the effort has gone into remembering rather than reading, and the research says that's the effort that makes the difference.
notice: How pupils react when the notes close. If they're reluctant to have a go without them, that often tells you they've mistaken familiarity for knowing.
What the checking stage turns up. The gaps pupils find for themselves here are the ones that re-reading would have hidden from them, so they're worth paying attention to.
Whether confidence and recall actually match up. Pupils who felt they knew the material from reading it can be surprised by how little of it they can produce when asked.
consider: This works best as a straight swap for re-reading rather than something extra on top. The time pupils would have spent going over their notes becomes the retrieval attempt plus the check, so it doesn't add anything to anyone's workload.

You can expect a bit of resistance at first, because retrieving feels harder than reading. That difficulty is normal, and the research suggests it's actually part of what makes the practice work, so it isn't a sign that something has gone wrong.
pages.wider: This is the testing effect, and it's one of the best evidenced findings in the guide. Roediger and Karpicke found that retrieval did more for retention weeks later than re-studying did, and Dunlosky's reviews rank practice testing among the most effective study techniques available.

why: Five questions at the start of the lesson, on things you've taught before, with nothing going in the gradebook. It doesn't look like much, and that's fine, because the value is in the routine. A little retrieval done regularly, lesson after lesson, does far more for remembering than the occasional big revision session.

The low stakes are doing a lot of the work too. Agarwal found that routine quizzing reduces test anxiety rather than causing it, because when it happens often and nothing rides on it, pupils stop seeing it as a threat and start treating it as practice. As the card says, the quiz is not the assessment. It is the learning.
example: A science class starts every lesson the same way, with five questions on the board covering earlier topics. Pupils answer from memory in the back of their books and self-mark in a minute or so. Nothing is collected in and nothing is graded. The teacher notes which questions caused trouble, and moves on.
pages.try: Pick one class and try five questions tomorrow, self-marked. It's absolutely fine to reuse questions from earlier lessons, because it's the doing it regularly that helps, far more than having fresh questions every time.
notice: Which questions the class keeps getting wrong. Those topics need reteaching, not just quizzing again.

Whether the routine feels low stakes to the pupils, not just on paper. You'll know Agarwal's finding is holding when pupils treat the quiz as a normal part of the lesson rather than something to worry about.
How long it actually takes. If the starter is swallowing fifteen minutes, it's usually the admin that needs trimming rather than the retrieval.
consider: Keeping it out of the gradebook isn't an optional extra. The low stakes are the reason the anxiety finding holds, so the moment marks ride on it, it becomes a different activity.
Self-marking keeps the workload at zero, and it puts the checking where it's most useful, in the pupil's own hands, straight away.
tech: This is a routine where the approved quiz or response tool in your setting can genuinely help, with quick starters every lesson, no marking, and results you can glance at while pupils move on. Let the tool look after the admin, the collecting in and the scoring, and keep the retrieval effort with the pupils. One thing to watch for is pace, because if it turns into a race, rewarding speed over thought, it takes away the very difficulty that makes the practice worthwhile.

stair.lede: Writing five fresh questions every lesson is the sort of drafting job AI does well, through the approved tool in your setting. This is Mark's own STAIR example for exactly this job:
stair.prompt:
Act as a primary teacher who is a science specialist. Create retrieval questions on the water cycle for Year 5. Keep tightly to evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection. Present the output in clearly labelled sections.

Pupils should be able to demonstrate confident explanations and supply short applied questions.

Every question must include plausible distractors based on age-appropriate misconceptions.

Keep all questions concise with no added detail, definitions or answers.
stair.after: Swap the role, topic and year group for your own, and then go back and forth with it until the questions match what you actually taught, because that's the I in STAIR. The judgement about which questions make the cut stays with you.

pages.wider: Roediger and Karpicke supply the memory case for frequent testing, and Agarwal's classroom studies supply the reassurance that quizzing, done routinely and without stakes, reduces test anxiety rather than feeding it.

why: Most revision defaults to putting information back in front of pupils, so they re-read, they highlight, and they copy out their notes. The research in this guide points the other way. Getting the knowledge out, retrieving it, does more for long term memory than another pass over the page.

A brain dump is the simplest possible version of that. It needs no preparation, no question writing and no technology, and it shows you something a quiz can't, which is what pupils reach for when nothing prompts them, and the order it comes out in.
example: Two lessons into a new topic, a class gets a blank page and two minutes to write down everything they can remember about last lesson, with no notes and no talking. Afterwards, pupils open their books and check what they missed. The teacher asks for one thing that didn't come back, and the answers help shape the start of the next lesson.
pages.try: Try ending one lesson this week with it. Give pupils two minutes and a blank page to write everything they can remember from today, and keep it out of any book you mark, because the value is in the retrieving rather than in the record it leaves.
notice: What most of the class couldn't recall. The card says it plainly: that is precisely where teaching needs to return.
Who writes steadily and who freezes at the blank page. Freezing tells you something useful too, and cued recall is a gentler step back for those pupils.
Whether what comes back is what you'd have predicted, because quite often it isn't.
consider: There has to be something there to retrieve. If pupils have only met the material once, a brain dump tells you more about the teaching so far than about the pupils.
The imperfect attempt is the point of the exercise, so try to resist tidying it up into a marked task. As soon as it carries stakes, pupils start playing safe, and you lose the honest picture.
pages.wider: This sits squarely in the testing effect tradition. Roediger and Karpicke showed that the act of retrieving is itself a learning event, and not just a way of measuring one.
tech: Paper does this job perfectly well. Where the approved shared document or whiteboard tool in your setting can add something is in the reading, because you can see thirty attempts at once and skim them for gaps without collecting in a single book. The retrieval effort is the important part though, not the admin around it.

why: Quizzing pupils on content you haven't taught them yet sounds backwards, but that is exactly what the card is describing. Struggling to retrieve primes the brain, and students who fail before instruction remember the answer more reliably once it's taught.
It's also a helpful way of thinking about failure, because here the wrong answers aren't a problem you have to manage. The struggle to answer is doing useful work before the teaching even starts.
example: Before a lesson introducing the causes of the First World War, a history teacher poses three questions the class can't yet answer well and asks for best guesses. There are no marks, and no discussion beyond a brief reveal. The lesson then teaches the material, and those early guesses give the new content something to attach itself to.
pages.try: Try opening one new topic with two or three questions pupils can't yet answer, asked for best guesses, before any of the teaching happens. Keep it brief, because it's the priming you're after rather than the scores.
notice: How pupils handle being asked about things they don't know yet. This only really works if guessing wrong is visibly safe in your classroom.
Whether the material you pre-tested comes back more reliably later on than material you introduced without the quiz.
consider: It's worth being explicit with the class about why you're doing it. Pupils who are told that failing here is productive respond really differently from pupils who suspect they're being caught out.
This pairs naturally with the generation effect, because a wrong answer generated before the right one is revealed is doing useful work for memory.
pages.wider: Bjork's work on pretesting and Kapur's on productive failure point the same way, which is that unsuccessful retrieval before instruction can prepare memory for what comes next.

why: Reconstruction sits somewhere between a brain dump and a formal test. Pupils rebuild the key ideas of a topic from memory, and then they open their notes and correct what they wrote in a different colour. Karpicke and Blunt found this does more for retention than re-reading.

The second colour is what makes it more than just a memory exercise. For the pupil, the corrections are a precise record of what didn't come back, and for you, they turn every page into something you can read at a glance.
example: At the end of a unit on rivers, pupils close their books and write out the processes of erosion from memory. Ten minutes later they open their notes and add whatever they missed in green pen. Flicking through the books afterwards, the teacher can see the same two processes missing in green across half the class.
pages.try: Try running it once at the end of a current topic, with pupils reconstructing from memory and then correcting in colour. The colour really does matter here, because without it the gaps just disappear into the page.
notice: Where the second colour clusters. Whole-class gaps give you a reteaching list, and it's one the pupils have written for you themselves.
Whether the corrections are additions or fixes, because missing knowledge and mangled knowledge need different responses from you.
consider: Try to resist marking the reconstruction itself. The imperfect first attempt is what makes it work, and stakes push pupils back towards playing safe.
The check against the notes is part of the learning rather than an admin step at the end, so give it proper time.
pages.wider: Karpicke and Blunt found that rebuilding a topic from memory outperformed re-reading for retention, even though the re-reading felt more productive at the time. It's the testing effect applied to whole topics rather than single questions.

why: Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve well over a century ago, and Cepeda's work put numbers on the gaps that help most. The finding hasn't really changed in all that time: retrieval spread across days and weeks does more for retention than the same amount of practice squeezed into one session.
The hard part isn't believing it, it's timetabling it, which is why the card aims this at your medium-term plan rather than your lesson plan. The calendar is part of the pedagogy.
example: Planning a six-week unit, a teacher pencils the review points in before the content, so week three revisits week one, week five revisits weeks two and three, and the following unit opens by retrieving this one. Nothing about any single lesson changes very much, but the shape of the term does.
pages.try: Take the medium-term plan for your next unit and mark two points where earlier content will come back. Booking the slots is the habit worth building, and the questions themselves can always be written later.
notice: What the first spaced review reveals. Material that seemed really secure at the time will have faded, and that's the forgetting curve doing what it does, not a failure of your teaching.
Whether the review points survive contact with a busy term. If they're the first thing to get cut, they were never really planned in at all.
consider: Massed practice feels better in the room, for you and for pupils, so expect the spaced version to look worse lesson by lesson while it does more across the term.
tech: Spaced repetition tools exist for exactly this problem. They bring older material back at the right intervals automatically, which matches what the research says while saving you the headache of tracking it all by hand. If your setting has an approved one, let it carry the scheduling. The intervals are a job the tool can do, but making sure that what comes back is worth retrieving is still yours.
pages.wider: Cepeda and colleagues put numbers on the gaps that Ebbinghaus first mapped, and Dunlosky's reviews place distributed practice in the top tier of study techniques.

why: Spacing retrieval out over time is one of the most robust findings in memory research, and it's also one of the hardest to do consistently, because it needs the calendar as much as it needs the lesson plan.

This routine gets around the consistency problem by making the spacing automatic. You ask three questions per lesson, at three different distances, and older material keeps coming back around without you having to track anything at all.
example: A geography teacher's starter slide carries the same three headings every lesson: yesterday, last week, last month. Writing tomorrow's slide is quick work with the medium term plan open, and pupils answer from memory before any books come out.
pages.try: Add the three headings to your existing starter template and fill them in for one class tomorrow. Getting the routine going helps far more than agonising over the perfect choice of questions.
notice: Which distance fails. If yesterday's question lands but last month's doesn't, that's the spacing doing its diagnostic job for you.
Whether the same older topic keeps failing. The card is explicit that the intervals are a starting point, and complex topics may well need revisiting more often.
consider: It only works if the older material genuinely comes back around, which makes this a planning habit as much as a lesson habit. The guide puts it well: the calendar is part of the pedagogy.
When content never returns after it's been taught, pupils decide it no longer matters. This routine is the antidote, but only if you protect it when time gets tight.
pages.wider: The spacing effect runs all the way from Ebbinghaus through to Cepeda's work on the best gaps to leave, and Dunlosky's reviews rank distributed practice among the most effective techniques available.
tech: A low-stakes quiz tool, the approved one in your setting, takes the marking out of this entirely and keeps the routine sustainable, and a spaced repetition tool can handle the intervals for you too. What no tool should do is soften the retrieval itself, because the struggle needs to stay with the learner.

stair.lede: Drafting three questions at three distances, every single lesson, is exactly the kind of repetitive drafting AI is good at, through the approved tool in your setting, and a STAIR-shaped prompt can do the heavy lifting:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary geography teacher. Create retrieval questions for a Year 8 class: one on yesterday's lesson (river landforms), one from last week (the water cycle), one from last month (map skills and grid references).

Keep every question answerable from memory in under a minute, focused on one precise idea, with no hints in the wording.

Keep the wording concise and do not include answers, explanations or extra detail.
stair.after: Swap in your own subject, class and topics, and expect to go back and forth a few times before it's right, because that's the I in STAIR and the iteration really is essential. You choose the questions, and the tool just drafts them.

why: Blocked practice, where you finish one topic before starting the next, feels organised, and pupils working through a block feel fluent. Kornell and Bjork found that the feeling misleads, because mixing topics up produces stronger retention than blocking them does.

The card names the mechanism: discriminating. When the question types arrive shuffled together, pupils have to decide first what kind of problem they're actually looking at, and that decision is exactly the one that blocked practice never asks them to make.
example: A maths teacher setting practice on area swaps a page of fifteen area questions for a mixed set, with area, perimeter and volume shuffled together. Pupils now have to choose the method before they can apply it. The work is slower and scrappier than the blocked version would be, but having to choose is the extra ingredient the blocked page was missing.
pages.try: Shuffle one existing practice set so that two or three related topics arrive mixed together. Topics pupils can genuinely confuse with each other give the discrimination something to bite on.
notice: Accuracy dipping during the practice. Kornell and Bjork's point is that the dip in the lesson and the gain in retention tend to arrive together.
Whether pupils pause to work out what kind of question they're looking at before answering it, because that little pause is exactly what the mixing is meant to bring about.
consider: Tell pupils why the practice feels harder. Without the explanation, interleaving can read as disorganisation, to them and sometimes to observers too.
pages.wider: Kornell and Bjork's studies established the effect, and it's Rohrer's work in mathematics classrooms that has tested it furthest from the laboratory.

why: The revision most pupils do by default, a single heavy session of re-reading close to the exam, is the pattern the evidence ranks lowest. Dunlosky's review placed re-reading among the least effective strategies there are, and as the card says, many students do the opposite of what works.

This strategy is a little unusual in this guide, because the audience for it is the pupils themselves. You teach them the schedule directly, which is to study something, come back to it after two days, then after a week, and then after a month. It's knowledge about learning, and it can be taught like any other knowledge.
example: Ahead of mocks, a form tutor walks the class through building a revision timetable that comes back to each subject at growing intervals, rather than blocking one subject per evening. Pupils compare the plan with how they revised last time, and most of them find they'd been doing the reverse.
pages.try: Next time you set revision, make the schedule part of the task itself, so pupils know which nights they're revising, what they're returning to, and how big the gaps are. The gap sizes are a starting point, and you can adjust them to fit your subject and your class.
notice: What pupils' current schedules actually look like. It's worth asking before you teach the alternative, because seeing the difference between the two is what tends to persuade them.
Whether the schedule survives when pupils are on their own, or collapses back into cramming. One walkthrough rarely changes habits all by itself, so expect to come back to it.
consider: Spacing feels less productive than cramming while you're actually doing it, and that's partly why pupils abandon it. Teaching the schedule works better when you also explain why it's going to feel wrong at first.
pages.wider: Dunlosky and colleagues reviewed ten common study techniques and placed distributed practice near the top and re-reading near the bottom. This strategy simply hands that finding to the people doing the revising.

why: When a topic is taught, assessed and never seen again, pupils draw the sensible conclusion that it no longer matters. The card is blunt about this, and the fix is structural rather than clever. You bring earlier content back in starters and assessments, and you plan for that at the level of the term rather than trying to improvise it lesson by lesson.

Cumulative review is really just spacing applied to your planning documents. Nothing new gets taught. What changes is that older material keeps its place in the room, so pupils keep meeting it and keep retrieving it.
example: A languages department agrees that every end-of-unit assessment will draw a quarter of its marks from earlier units, so vocabulary from September keeps appearing in January. Pupils stop treating each unit as something to be finished with, because they can see for themselves that it isn't.
pages.try: Look at your next planned assessment and add a small section drawn from a previous unit. It's worth announcing it in advance too, because the aim is to change what pupils keep revisiting, not to catch them out.
notice: How pupils respond when old content reappears. If they're surprised, that tells you they'd already decided the old material was finished with, which is exactly the expectation you're working on.
Which earlier topics have faded furthest, because those are the ones to bring back first.
consider: A question bank grows more useful every term you do this. Writing cumulative questions from scratch every time adds workload, and it's the sort of workload that gets this dropped in a busy year, so build the bank as you go and let it accumulate.
pages.wider: Bjork's spacing research explains why the planned reappearances help, and Carey, the card's other source, makes the same case for building the return into the plan rather than leaving it to chance.

why: This is the idea that sits underneath the whole retrieval guide, so it's worth taking a moment on it. The conditions that make learning feel hard and slow in the moment, such as spacing it out, mixing it up and testing rather than reviewing, are often the very conditions that make it last. And the conditions that feel smooth and productive tend to give pupils confidence without much retention to back it up.

That runs against every instinct in a helpful profession. When a pupil struggles to retrieve something, the natural move is to make it easier with a hint, a prompt or a quicker reveal. Bjork's work suggests the struggle is doing useful work, provided that what's being asked for was genuinely taught in the first place.
example: A teacher running a retrieval quiz turns the hints off and lets the silence run a little longer before revealing the answers. Pupils grumble that it feels harder than last term's version, and it is. But weeks later, it's the harder version they can still remember.
pages.try: Take one retrieval activity you already run and remove one support from it, such as the hints, the word bank, or the notes-open first pass. Change nothing else, so you can see what the added difficulty actually does for your class.
notice: The gap between how the activity feels and what it produces. If pupils rate it as harder but recall more later on, that's the effect working just as described.
Confident wrong answers. These are worth watching for, because difficulty brings the illusion of knowing out into the open, and smooth practice tends to leave it hidden.
consider: Desirable difficulty isn't the same thing as confusion. Difficulty that comes from an unclear task or untaught content is just a barrier, so the struggle has to be in the retrieving, not in working out what's being asked.

Secure the foundations first, because effortful retrieval works on knowledge that actually exists. That's why the guide pairs this idea with checking the basics are in place before pushing beyond them.
How long to let the struggle run isn't a rule anyone can hand you. It's a judgement made in the room, by the teacher who knows these students, watching whether the effort is still productive.
pages.wider: Bjork coined the phrase desirable difficulties for exactly this pattern, and the EEF's cognitive science review is a fair guide to how far the laboratory findings have travelled into real classrooms.
tech: The card's tech line says it all: any retrieval tool, hints disabled. If the approved tool in your setting rewards speed, streaks or fastest-finger reveals, it's taking away the very difficulty that makes the practice worthwhile, so those settings are worth checking before you rely on it.

why: Retrieval with notes open is reading, not retrieval. The card's line is worth keeping whole, because it describes something that happens in plenty of well-intentioned classrooms, where the activity looks like a quiz but the notes on the desk are doing the remembering.

The answer isn't to ban support. It's to fade it on a schedule, so notes first, then headings only, then nothing at all. The move to unaided retrieval is where the memory gets its strengthening, so the fade deserves as much planning as the support did.
example: Reviewing a topic across three lessons, a teacher runs the same retrieval task each time with a little less on the table, so full notes in the first lesson, a five-heading skeleton in the second, and a blank page in the third. The questions stay the same all the way through. It's only the support that shrinks.
pages.try: Take a retrieval activity your class currently does with the notes open, and run it next time with headings only. One step of the fade is plenty to start with, and you can see how it goes from there.
notice: What happens at each step down. A sharp drop between the notes and the headings tells you the notes were doing the remembering, which is useful to know.
Who freezes when the last support goes. Cued recall is a gentler step back for those pupils, so nobody has to jump straight to the blank page.
consider: How fast to fade is a judgement made in the room. The teacher who knows the class can see whether the struggle is still productive, and no schedule on a website can make that call for you.
Support removed too early produces confusion rather than desirable difficulty. The struggle has to be in the retrieving, not in guessing what's wanted.
tech: If you use an approved quiz tool for retrieval, its settings are part of the fade too, so hints off, closed-book or timed mode on, and anything that supplies the answer at the first hesitation switched off. Let the tool run the activity for you, but keep the struggle with the pupils.
pages.wider: Bjork's desirable difficulties frame the case for withdrawing support, and Kornell's work with him on how learners misread easy practice explains why the faded version feels worse than it really is.

why: There are lots of ways knowledge can get stuck in the format it was practised in. A pupil who can answer a question in a quiz can really struggle to recognise the same question when it turns up in an essay, and it's not that the knowledge isn't there, it's that it's tied to the situation they learned it in.

Godden and Baddeley showed decades ago that recall is bound to context. The card's response is to retrieve the same content in different formats and settings, so the knowledge gradually comes loose from any one of them. It does make things harder for students, but this is one of those places where the harder version is the one doing them some good.
example: One week a class retrieves the digestive system by labelling a diagram, the next by writing a paragraph from memory, and later on by answering spoken questions with no image in sight. The content stays exactly the same each time, and it's just the format around it that keeps moving.
pages.try: Take some content the class has only ever retrieved one way and switch the format once, such as diagram to prose, written to spoken, or multiple choice to free recall. See what travels and what doesn't.
notice: How pupils do when the format changes. Some drop in performance is completely normal, and it shows you how much of the knowledge was tied to the old format.
Whose knowledge already travels across formats and whose is bound to just one. For that second group, it's worth remembering they may have learned the format as much as the content.
consider: Vary the retrieval rather than the goal. What's being retrieved stays the same, and it's only the packaging around it that moves, because otherwise you're testing something new rather than strengthening something taught.
pages.wider: Godden and Baddeley's diving study is the classic demonstration that recall is tied to the context it was learned in, and Bjork's work on varied practice shows how teachers can put that finding to use.

why: Slamecka and Graf found that generating an answer before being told it, even a wrong answer, produces stronger retention than passive exposure does. The wrong answers part is worth sitting with for a moment, because it's the effort of coming up with an attempt that does the good, not whether the attempt was right.

In practice, this is the finding that makes it worth asking before telling. Whenever the answer arrives before pupils have had a go at one of their own, that useful effort simply never happens, and it costs almost nothing to let it happen.
example: Introducing a new French verb, the teacher shows the infinitive and asks the class to guess the first-person form before revealing it. Half the guesses are wrong, but every pupil now has an attempt of their own to compare the answer against, and that comparison is where the learning gets its grip.
pages.try: Build one ask-before-tell moment into an explanation you already give, so pose the question, take some guesses, and then reveal. It only costs you a few seconds, and you can use it almost anywhere.
notice: Whether pupils will actually commit to a guess. A class that's been trained to wait for the answer will need convincing that wrong attempts are genuinely welcome, so it can take a little while to bed in.
What the wrong guesses tell you about how pupils are thinking, because they're useful evidence for you as well as useful effort for them.
consider: The attempt has to come before the answer, not instead of it. Generation works because the correction follows, and leaving errors uncorrected is a different activity with different risks.
pages.wider: Slamecka and Graf named the generation effect in the 1970s, and McDaniel's work has since carried it into more realistic educational materials.

why: The instinct after teaching something is to check it straight away, while it's fresh. The trouble is that a quiz straight after teaching mostly confirms what was said a few minutes ago, rather than telling you what's actually been learned. The card is direct about the alternative: wait a day, then quiz. Wait a week, then quiz again.
A little forgetting first makes the retrieval effortful, and that effort is what strengthens the memory. So the gap isn't dead time before the real work. The gap is doing some of the work.
example: A teacher finishes explaining photosynthesis and, instead of quizzing on it in the plenary, quizzes on last week's respiration work instead. Photosynthesis gets its first quiz tomorrow, and its second the following week.
pages.try: Move one end-of-lesson quiz to the start of the next lesson. Nothing else needs to change except the gap, which makes this one of the easier things in the guide to try.
notice: Scores dropping compared with same-lesson quizzing. That's expected, and it's actually the reason for the change, because the quiz is now measuring what's remembered rather than what's still echoing from the lesson.
Whether the week-later quiz shows the material coming back more securely than the day-later one did, because that's the spacing beginning to pay off.
consider: It's worth explaining the delay to pupils too. The gap is a deliberate choice, and knowing that can help the harder quiz feel fair rather than punitive.
Checking understanding within the lesson still has its place, and that's formative assessment doing a different job. It's the retrieval practice that waits.
pages.wider: Bjork's work on spacing and Roediger's on the testing effect come together here, because a test strengthens memory most when a little forgetting has been allowed to happen first.

why: Retrieval is not a pub quiz. The card's warning is aimed at a drift that's easy to fall into, where retrieval routines settle permanently at the level of dates, definitions and labelled diagrams, simply because those questions are the easiest ones to write and mark.

Agarwal's work behind this card cuts both ways though. Factual retrieval builds the foundations, so it isn't beneath anyone, and higher-order retrieval then checks whether students can actually use what all those facts add up to. Secure the foundations first, then push beyond them.
example: After several factual quizzes on the causes of the Wall Street Crash, a history teacher's retrieval question changes shape, and pupils are asked which cause mattered most, argued from memory in five sentences. The facts they've been retrieving for weeks become the material for a judgement.
pages.try: Have a look at a week of your retrieval questions and ask yourself a simple question: could pupils answer these without understanding the topic? Then add one question that asks them to use the knowledge rather than just produce it.
notice: Pupils who are fluent in the factual rounds but stall when asked to apply. The knowledge may well be there, and it's the using of it that's unpractised.
What your question mix has drifted towards over a term. It's worth actually checking rather than assuming, because the drift is usually invisible from the inside.
consider: The order matters here. Higher-order retrieval on insecure foundations produces guessing rather than thinking, so the card's sequence, foundations first, is there for a reason.
pages.wider: Agarwal's studies of factual and higher-order quizzing sit directly behind this card, and they belong to the testing effect tradition that runs from Roediger and Karpicke onwards.

why: The important part of this one is the from-memory bit. Concept mapping with the notes open is an organising task, and a perfectly good one, but concept mapping from memory is retrieval, and Karpicke and Blunt found it outperformed re-reading for retention.

It also retrieves something a quiz rarely touches, which is the connections, so not just what students know but how the ideas relate to each other. As the card has it, relational knowledge beats isolated facts.
example: Closing a unit on ecosystems, pupils get a blank page and one instruction, which is to map the topic from memory, with the ideas in boxes and the relationships written on the lines between them. Books stay shut the whole time. Afterwards they compare maps in pairs and add the missing links in another colour.
pages.try: Run one from-memory map at the end of a current topic, and ask for the connecting lines to be labelled, because a labelled line means the relationship has actually been retrieved rather than just implied.
notice: The links, even more than the boxes. Missing ideas show gaps in the knowledge, and missing links show gaps in how it all fits together, which is often the more useful thing to know.
Whether the maps improve across the year. Mapping is a skill in itself, so early attempts will understate what pupils actually know, and that's worth allowing for.
consider: The from-memory condition is what makes it work, so try to resist the merciful instinct to allow a quick peek at the notes. The checking comes afterwards, as its own step, and it's better for being separate.
pages.wider: Karpicke and Blunt's study is the direct source here, and it belongs to the broader testing effect tradition established by Roediger and Karpicke.

why: Anyone who has prepared to teach a topic will know that moment, halfway through the preparation, of discovering what they don't actually know. Preparing to teach demands complete, organised retrieval, and the gaps a quiz might skirt around become impossible to ignore when the whole thing has to be explained in order.

The card's emphasis is worth holding on to, which is that the learning happens during the preparation rather than the delivery. Organising knowledge so you can explain it to someone else is where the consolidation happens, and that's true whether or not the explaining ever takes place.
example: Pairs in a physics class each prepare a three-minute explanation of one circuit concept for another pair, from memory, with one diagram allowed. Most of the retrieval work is done before anyone speaks, in deciding what comes first, what connects to what, and what they had to go back and check.
pages.try: Set preparing-to-teach as the task, without necessarily running the teaching itself. Planning an explanation of last month's topic is a complete retrieval activity all on its own.
notice: What pupils look up while they're preparing, because every check against the notes is a gap they've found for themselves.
The order pupils choose to explain things in. The sequencing choices show you how their knowledge is organised, which is hard to see any other way.
consider: Delivery adds a pressure that preparation doesn't, and whether a class is ready for peer teaching is your call, not the strategy's. The preparation on its own still does most of the good.
pages.wider: Nestojko and colleagues found that merely expecting to teach changes how people study, and Fiorella and Mayer's work on learning by teaching locates the benefit in the organising and explaining itself.

why: Between showing pupils the answer and asking for it cold, there's a wide and really useful middle ground. Tulving and Thomson showed that retrieval depends on the cues available, and a heading, a keyword or a diagram with its labels removed can each trigger retrieval without doing the remembering for the pupil.

The important thing is that cued recall is a step on the way rather than a place to stop. It builds confidence before unaided retrieval, and it's a gentler way back in for pupils who freeze at a blank page.
example: A pupil who produced almost nothing in a free brain dump gets the same task again with the topic's five subheadings printed down the margin. The headings cue what order things come in, but the remembering in between them is still the pupil's own.
pages.try: Keep a cued version of your usual retrieval task ready, so the same questions with a keyword or a first letter alongside. Moving one pupil down to it costs you nothing, and it keeps everyone retrieving.
notice: Which cues bring the memory back and which just draw blank looks, because a cue that does nothing suggests the memory it points at was never secure in the first place.
Who still needs the cues after several rounds. The aim is to retire them gradually, pupil by pupil, rather than all at once.
consider: Cues can drift into being answers. A sentence starter that contains the key term has crossed the line from triggering the retrieval to replacing it, so it's worth checking your cues now and again.
Pair this with a plan to fade the cues away, because cued recall that never becomes unaided recall stops short of where the consolidation happens.

stair.lede: Turning your notes into gapped versions is repetitive drafting work, which makes it a fair job for AI through the approved tool in your setting:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary history teacher. Take the key points below about the causes of the First World War and create a gapped version for Year 9 cued recall, removing one key term per sentence and listing the removed words separately.

Keep every sentence otherwise word for word as supplied. Do not add new content, explanations or answers beside the gaps.

[paste your key points here]
stair.after: Because the tool only removes words from text you supply, what pupils retrieve is still exactly what you taught. Check that the gaps target the terms that carry the meaning, and go back and forth with it if they don't, because they often won't be right first time.

pages.wider: Tulving and Thomson's encoding specificity work established that what can be recalled depends on the cues present at retrieval, and this strategy simply puts that finding to deliberate use.
tech: A cloze quiz or gapped handout tool, the approved one in your setting, builds the cued step really quickly and lets you fade the cues over successive attempts too.

why: Pupils' judgements of what they know tend to be off, and mostly off in one direction. Familiar material feels known, and Koriat and Bjork traced how that feeling misleads. The result is revision effort spent in all the wrong places, by pupils who genuinely believe they're revising well.

You can't simply lecture the illusion away. The card's move is to let pupils catch themselves in it, by rating their confidence before the answer is revealed and then looking at where the certainty and the correctness came apart. The moments when they were certain and wrong are exactly the ones to spend time on.
example: Before each answer in a quiz review is revealed, pupils hold up one to five fingers to show their confidence. On question four, half the class shows five fingers and the revealed answer proves most of them wrong, so the teacher stops the quiz right there, and that question, rather than the quiz score, becomes the discussion.
pages.try: Add a confidence rating to one quiz you already run, and a simple scale of sure, unsure or guessing is plenty. The comparison with the revealed answers does most of the teaching for you.
notice: Where high confidence meets wrong answers, because those items are what this whole strategy is aiming at.
Whether the calibration improves over the weeks. Fewer certain-and-wrong moments is what progress looks like here, and it tends to come gradually.
consider: Confident errors want fast correction, and Metcalfe's finding on instant feedback applies most exactly here.

It may be worth keeping the ratings private at first, if being wrong in public carries a social cost in this class. That's a judgement for the teacher who knows the room, because you can see whether this class can be wrong out loud, and no guide can see that for you.
pages.wider: Koriat and Bjork documented the illusion of knowing, and Dunlosky's metacognition research shows just how loosely felt confidence tracks actual retention.

why: This card carries two instructions at once, and that's deliberate. Metcalfe shows that instant feedback is essential for confident errors, because the more certain a pupil was, the more the fast correction helps. For general retrieval though, it's worth leaving a little gap before revealing the answers, so the retrieval attempt has room to finish.
So the rule the card offers is really about knowing when to be quick. Speed matters most when the confidence is highest, and the rest of the time a pause does no harm at all.
example: Running a review quiz, a teacher reveals each answer a beat or two after the question rather than instantly, which lets pupils commit to an answer. When a show of hands turns up a confidently wrong majority on one item, the delay disappears and that misconception gets corrected on the spot.
pages.try: Next quiz, delay each reveal until every pupil has committed to an answer, and then break your own rule the moment you spot a confident error.
notice: What pupils do in the gap before the reveal. If they're reconsidering and committing, the gap is being used well, and if they're just waiting, it isn't doing much for them.
Whether the corrected confident errors stay corrected the following week. Metcalfe's work suggests they often may, and it's worth seeing whether that holds for your class.
consider: Instant feedback and instant answers are different things. Feedback follows an attempt, and a tool that supplies the answer at the first pause has replaced the attempt altogether.
tech: Quiz tools with instant answer reveal are built for exactly half of this card. The reveal speed is usually a setting, so it's worth checking whether the approved tool in your setting can hold the answers back until the responses are in. And if the format starts to resemble a fastest finger first round, rewarding speed over thought, it's taking away the difficulty that makes the retrieval worth doing.
pages.wider: Metcalfe's research on error correction is the direct source for the card's distinction, including the finding that high-confidence errors are especially correctable.

why: Students tend to be most confident about the things they read most recently, not the things they actually know. That's Dunlosky and Metcalfe's finding, and it explains a great deal of misdirected revision, because recently-seen material feels secure, and pupils make their revision decisions on that feeling.

Rating confidence after each retrieval attempt, and then revealing the answer, turns that private feeling into something that can actually be checked. What you're looking for is the gap between the rating and the result.
example: In a self-quizzing routine, pupils answer each question, write 1 to 5 for how sure they are, and then check. One pupil finds her 5s are mostly right, but so are her 2s. She knows more than she feels she does, and her revision list changes accordingly.
pages.try: Add a one-number confidence column to any answer-then-check activity the class already does. It only takes a few seconds per question, and the pattern builds up quickly.
notice: Patterns that keep repeating, such as pupils who are always certain and pupils who are never certain. Both are calibration problems, and they need different conversations.
Whether the ratings change what pupils choose to revise. The number is only worth collecting if it changes a decision somewhere.
consider: Rate after the attempt, not before it. The card is specific about this, because the attempt itself is evidence the rating should draw on.
pages.wider: Dunlosky and Metcalfe's work on metacognitive monitoring is the direct source here, and their finding is that judgements of learning track recency and fluency more faithfully than they track actual knowledge.

why: Most retrieval activity leaves nothing behind. The quiz happened, some things came back and some didn't, and by next week nobody, the pupil included, can remember which was which.

A retrieval journal keeps that record of what came back, what didn't, and what needs revisiting. Zimmerman showed that students who monitor their performance make better revision decisions, and the card frames the journal accordingly: it is a map of what to do next, not a diary.
example: After each Friday quiz, pupils spend three minutes on a simple two-column log, with what came back on one side and what didn't on the other. The did-not column from the last month becomes their personal starter list for revision week, and no teacher marking is involved at any point.
pages.try: Two columns in the back of the exercise book is a complete version of this, so you can start after your next retrieval activity with no preparation at all.
notice: Whether the journal actually changes what pupils do. A log nobody looks back at is just admin, and the real test is what pupils choose to revisit.
Entries that keep appearing in the did-not column. If a pupil logs the same content as missing three times, that's useful information for you as well as for them.
consider: Keep the logging light. Three minutes of honest record does more good than ten minutes of carefully presented reflection, and marking it changes what pupils are willing to write down.
pages.wider: Zimmerman's self-regulation research supplies the case for the monitoring, and Dunlosky's reviews supply the strategies the journal should steer pupils towards.

why: Dunlosky's review rated ten common study strategies, and re-reading scored low while practice testing scored highest. Most pupils have never seen that table, and you can usually tell, because their revision defaults to the strategies at the bottom of it.
The strategy is a structured comparison, so you ask students how they revise, and then you show them the evidence. As the card puts it, that conversation is the intervention.
example: Before study leave, a tutor group lists their revision methods anonymously on slips. The tally goes up on the board next to a summary of Dunlosky's ratings, and re-reading and highlighting dominate the class list while sitting near the bottom of the evidence table. The session is spent on the gap between the two columns.
notice: The reasons pupils give for their current habits. It feels productive and I have always done it this way come up again and again, and they're worth naming aloud, because the desirable difficulties research explains exactly why effective practice doesn't feel effective.
Whether anything shifts by the next audit. It's worth running twice a year, because the second tally shows you whether the conversation changed anything.
consider: The point isn't to make pupils feel bad about their current habits but to give them something better, so pair the audit with teaching an alternative, such as the retrieval schedule, and the conversation ends with something to actually do.
pages.wider: Dunlosky and colleagues' review of ten study techniques is the whole evidence base here, and the audit simply puts its findings in front of the people they're about.

why: It's really easy for a class to finish every task you set and still miss the learning those tasks were there for. The intention is what you want them to learn, and the task is just the vehicle for it, but when the two blur together, pupils start judging success by whether they've finished, and in the rush of a busy lesson it's easy for the teacher to do the same.
Keeping the two separate changes lots of small, practical things, such as how you introduce the work, what you praise while pupils are getting on with it, and what you actually check at the end.
example: In history, the task might be a paragraph on the causes of the First World War, but the intention is to understand how long term tensions and short term triggers interact. The teacher frames the paragraph as one way of showing that understanding, and the check at the end of the lesson asks about the interaction rather than whether the paragraph got finished.
pages.try: In your next plan, try writing the intention and the task on separate lines. If you find you can't state the intention without describing the task, that's really worth a second look before the lesson.
notice: What pupils say when you ask them what they're learning. 'A poster' is a task answer, and the idea behind the poster is the learning answer.
Whether your own checks at the end of the lesson are assessing the learning or just the completion.
consider: The card asks for the separation at every stage, in your planning and in what you say to pupils, and it's easiest to hold on to at the start of a lesson and easiest to lose in the middle of a busy one.
pages.wider: Clarifying learning intentions is the first of Wiliam's formative assessment strands, and the important thing is that the answer to where the learner is going is about the learning rather than the activity.

why: When you hand criteria to a class, they arrive as your words, and your words carry your understanding rather than theirs. Asking pupils what excellent looks like before they begin means they have to do the analysis for themselves, and the card is really plain about why: criteria they articulate themselves land far more deeply than criteria handed to them.
The discussion is evidence in its own right too. What a class can and can't name about quality tells you what they can and can't yet see in good work.
example: Before a piece of persuasive writing, the class reads a strong letter and lists what makes it work. The teacher collects the suggestions, tidies up the overlaps, and the list on the board, in the pupils' own phrasing, becomes the checklist they draft against.
pages.try: Next time you'd normally put up a success criteria slide, hold it back. Ask the class first, and see how much of your slide they can build without you.
notice: The gap between what pupils suggest and what you would have written. The missing criteria show you what they can't yet recognise in good work.
Whether pupils actually refer back to the list while they're working, or whether it just stays on the board as decoration.
consider: Their language becoming the standard doesn't mean any list will do. You're still steering, collecting and sharpening and adding the things the class can't yet name, so the final criteria end up both theirs and right.
This pairs really naturally with exemplars, because criteria are so much easier for pupils to generate from work they can actually see than from a blank instruction.
pages.wider: Wiliam and Leahy include co-constructed criteria among their practical techniques for clarifying and sharing what quality means, so that the standard is understood rather than just displayed.

why: Rubrics describe quality, but exemplars actually show it. A pupil can read 'uses precise vocabulary' and nod along without any real idea of what precision looks like in this subject at this level, but put two pieces of work side by side and the difference becomes something they can point at.

There's a second advantage the card names too, which is that pupils spot quality in someone else's work far more readily than in their own, so judging an exemplar is really useful rehearsal for judging themselves.
example: Before a design evaluation, a technology teacher puts two anonymised evaluations from a previous year under the visualiser, one strong and one mid-standard. Pupils work out the differences in pairs, and those differences become the criteria for their own writing.
pages.try: Save two or three anonymised pieces from this year's classes. That's the whole preparation done, and next year's lesson starts with them.
notice: The features pupils spot without being prompted, and the ones they miss entirely, because what they miss is what still needs teaching.
Whether the qualities they named in the exemplar actually show up in their own work afterwards.
consider: The card says work at different standards, not just a single model of excellence, and the contrast between the pieces is where the noticing happens.
Use work from other classes or previous years where you can. Whether a current pupil's work can be shown, even anonymised, is a judgement for the teacher who knows the class.
pages.wider: Sadler argued that pupils can only close a gap in quality they can actually perceive, and Berger's work on models of excellence makes the same case from the classroom, with standards caught from real work rather than from descriptions of it.

why: Copying an objective from the board at the start of a lesson produces writing rather than thinking. Asking pupils to name what they've learned at the end asks for both, because they have to look back over the lesson and come up with the answer for themselves.

It also gives you a small piece of evidence you simply can't get any other way, which is whether what they think the lesson was about matches what you think you taught, and the two aren't always the same.
example: At the end of a science lesson, pupils write one sentence on what today was actually about, and the teacher reads a handful aloud. Half the class describe the activity rather than the idea behind it, which tells the teacher exactly what to sharpen up next lesson.
pages.try: Once this week, try skipping the copied objective and asking for the sentence at the end instead. Then compare what they write with what you'd planned on the board.
notice: Answers that describe the task rather than the learning. The guide draws that line deliberately: finishing the task is not the same as achieving the learning.
How close the class's version is to yours. A wide gap isn't a failed lesson, it's just unusually honest feedback on the teaching.
consider: Withholding the objective isn't the same as hiding the point. Pupils still need to be clear about what they're doing and why while they work, and what changes is who puts the learning into words, and when.

Some schools expect objectives to be visible in every lesson, and how this routine sits with that expectation is a judgement for the teacher in the room. You know your class and your context better than any guide does.
pages.wider: The mechanism here is the generation effect: Slamecka and Graf found that producing an answer embeds it more reliably than copying one, even when the answer you produce needs correcting.

why: Every lesson has a turning point where you decide, usually on a feeling, whether the class is ready to move on. A hinge question swaps that feeling for evidence, with one diagnostic question, placed at the hinge, answered by everyone.

What makes it a hinge question rather than just a question is the way the wrong answers are designed. Each one maps to a misconception you already know pupils hold, so the spread of responses tells you not just how many are stuck but why they're stuck.
example: A maths teacher planning a lesson on adding fractions writes one question for the midpoint, with four responses: the right answer, the classic add-tops-and-bottoms error, a common denominator slip, and a simplification mistake. Every pupil answers at once on whiteboards, and the spread across the room decides the second half of the lesson.
pages.try: Plan a single hinge question for one lesson next week. Write the wrong answers first, from the errors you already see in books, and then build the question around them.
notice: Which distractor gets chosen, because that's the diagnosis, and it's much more useful than the count of correct answers.
What you actually did next. As the guide has it, evidence has done nothing until it changes what happens in the following five minutes.
consider: The card's warning really does deserve its own line: never improvise it. An improvised hinge question just collapses into a recall check with no diagnostic power.
It needs an all-pupil response method to work, because a hinge answered by three volunteers is a hinge in name only.
One good hinge per lesson is plenty. The cost is planning time, which is exactly why the wrong answers are worth engineering carefully once and then reusing.
pages.wider: This comes from Dylan Wiliam's formative assessment work, where assessment moves out of the marking pile and into the lesson, while it can still change the teaching.
tech: A polling or quiz tool, the approved one in your setting, can get you the whole room's answer at the hinge in seconds, with the spread visible straight away. The important thing is that the tool has done nothing until what it shows changes your next five minutes.

stair.lede: The expensive part of a hinge question is drafting distractors that map to real misconceptions, and AI, through the approved tool in your setting, can draft them for you to judge. A STAIR-shaped prompt looks like this:
stair.prompt:
Act as a primary teacher who is a science specialist and create hinge questions on the water cycle for Year 5. Keep tightly to evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection.

Present the output in clearly labelled sections and ensure each hinge question is quick to answer, focused on one precise idea and suitable as a decision point in the lesson. Ensure questions elicit the ability for Year 5 to apply their understanding with confidence.

Every hinge question must include plausible distractors based on age-appropriate misconceptions so teachers can interpret pupils' thinking accurately. Keep the wording concise and avoid unnecessary detail, explanations or answers.
stair.after: Swap the role, topic and year group for your own, and then do the part only you can do, which is checking each distractor against the misconceptions your pupils actually hold and iterating until they match. That's the I in STAIR, and it's the bit the diagnostic power depends on.

why: A multiple choice question with throwaway wrong answers only really tells you one thing, right or wrong. When it comes to engineering each distractor to map onto a real misconception though, the same question tells you why a pupil is wrong, which is the information you can actually teach from. As the card has it, wrong answers are the diagnostic data.
example: For a question on photosynthesis, a science teacher writes three distractors from errors seen in books, such as plants getting their food from the soil, plants only respiring at night, and oxygen being what plants take in rather than give out. Whichever option a pupil picks, the teacher knows which idea to go back to.
pages.try: Take one question you already use and rewrite its wrong answers from the errors in your current marking. The misconceptions are already there in the books, and the work is simply moving them into the options.
notice: Which distractor draws the most pupils, because the pattern is more useful than the score.
A distractor nobody ever picks. It tells you nothing at all, so replace it with an error pupils actually make.
Whether the same misconception comes back weeks later. A question worth engineering once is worth reusing.
consider: This is where the planning cost of a hinge question lives, and it's why the card treats the wrong answers as carefully as the right one. Improvised distractors just collapse the diagnosis.
tech: The approved quiz tool in your setting that shows the full spread of responses, not just the proportion correct, is what turns carefully built distractors into evidence, because you can see at a glance which misconception the room holds, and you see it from every pupil at once rather than the few who would have spoken. The important thing is that the chart has done nothing until it changes what you teach in the next five minutes.
pages.wider: Diagnostic questioning built on known misconceptions runs right through Black and Wiliam's account of eliciting evidence, and the point of asking is to find out what pupils actually think rather than to confirm what you hope they think.

why: Hands up only ever samples the confident. Random selection is fairer, but it's still chance, and chance can leave the same pupils unheard for weeks. Choosing who answers on purpose lets you reach the thinking you most need to hear, such as the pupil whose book worried you, or the one who hasn't spoken since Tuesday.
Tracking participation is what keeps the deliberateness honest. Memory flatters, but a record shows you who has actually stayed invisible across lessons.
example: A teacher keeps a simple tally of who has answered across the week. Before Friday's lesson she reads it back, finds three pupils with no entries at all, and plans a question for each of them, matched to material they've had time to think about.
pages.try: For one class, track who answers for a week, by whatever means is least effort. Read the record back before planning the next lesson and let it choose two of your questions for you.
notice: Who the record says you haven't heard from, because it's rarely who you would have guessed.
How the responses change once the class knows anyone might be asked, not just the raised hands.
consider: 'Where appropriate' is doing real work in the card. Which pupils to press, and when a quieter route to a pupil's thinking serves better than a public question, is a call for the teacher who knows the class, not a website.
tech: An approved participation tracking tool in your setting can carry the record for you, and its contribution is memory rather than judgement. It shows you who has stayed invisible across lessons, but deciding who to call, and why, stays with you.
pages.wider: Hearing from all learners rather than a self-selecting few is central to Wiliam and Black's case for assessment that happens during the lesson, while it can still change the teaching.

why: The classic weakness of classroom questioning is that you hear from a handful of pupils and make assumptions about everyone else. Mini whiteboards take the assumption away, because every pupil answers, every answer is visible, and you can read the whole room in seconds.
They change who participates too. There's no waiting for a turn and no hiding behind the confident few, which is why this one strategy turns up in so many of the routes through this site.
example: A languages teacher checking verb endings asks the class to write the conjugation and hold their boards up together on a count of three. Thirty answers appear at once, two errors dominate, and so the next five minutes deal with those two errors rather than moving on.
pages.try: Try one all-write, all-show question at tomorrow's key checkpoint. Showing together really matters, because staggered reveals let pupils copy the early boards.
notice: The answers from pupils you would never have called on, because that's the evidence you've been missing.
How quickly you can read the room, and what you do when the room disagrees with your plan.
consider: Boards suit short-form answers, so for extended reasoning you'll need a different route to the same visibility.
The point is the evidence, not the equipment. If the routine drifts into a game of speed, the quality of the answers goes with it, and so does the diagnosis.
pages.wider: Eliciting evidence from every pupil is one of Wiliam and Black's core formative assessment moves, and the whiteboard is simply the cheapest reliable way of doing it.
tech: Multimodal response tools, through the approved tool in your setting, do the same job when you need typed answers, anonymity or a record, with every learner visible at once. The test is exactly the same either way, because a screen full of responses has done nothing until it changes what you do next.

why: Four cards per pupil, one question, and every answer in the air at once. The routine costs almost nothing, and what it buys is the thing this strand keeps coming back to, a response from everyone rather than a guess about the room built from three raised hands.
No hands and no opt-out changes what answering feels like too. Nobody is volunteering, everyone is simply answering, and that lowers the cost of being wrong in front of others.
example: A geography teacher poses a four-option question on reading a population pyramid. On a count of three, thirty cards go up, and a visible cluster on option C, the misread axis, decides what gets explained next.
pages.try: A class set costs one preparation session, so print them, laminate them if you like, and keep them in the room. Then start with a single question at one checkpoint tomorrow.
notice: The spread, not just the most common answer, because a room split two ways needs different teaching from a room that is mostly right.
Pupils who glance sideways before raising their card. Everyone showing at the same time is what protects the evidence.
consider: The question has to deserve the routine. Four options invite properly engineered distractors, and a question with three filler answers wastes the whole-class machinery.
Cards suit selected response, so when you need to see working or prose, mini whiteboards or another route to the same full visibility does that job instead.
pages.wider: All-student response is one of Wiliam's staple techniques for eliciting evidence, so the next teaching decision gets made on the whole room rather than a sample of it.

why: Whatever method you use to gather responses decides, before any pupil even starts answering, who gets to show what they know. Oral questioning favours the quick and the confident, written answers favour fluent writers, and a single fixed method excludes the same pupils every time.

Offering written, verbal, visual and digital routes isn't variety for its own sake. It's about the evidence, because a pupil who can't respond through the channel you chose reads as not knowing, when the truth may be that they simply couldn't show it.
example: Checking understanding of a novel's turning point, a teacher accepts a sentence, a labelled sketch of the scene, or a short spoken answer on a class device. Two pupils who rarely write anything hand in sketches the teacher can read as evidence just like any written answer.
pages.try: Pick one routine check you already run and offer a second way of answering it. Even just one alternative channel is enough to see who it reaches.
notice: Which pupils change when the channel changes, because that difference is information about the method rather than the pupil.
Whether anonymity shifts the honesty of what comes back, especially on questions about confusion.
consider: More channels means more to read, so choose the checkpoints where the evidence justifies it rather than multiplying options in every task.
Which pupils need which route, and when a pupil should be stretched beyond a comfortable channel, is the teacher's call. The card sets the principle, not the prescription.
tech: Multimodal and anonymous response tools, the approved ones in your setting, are where this principle most obviously meets technology, because they can gather a response from every learner at once, in more than one form, and anonymity can make honest answers easier to give. The test stays the same as for every tool in this strand, which is that the responses only count as formative once they change what you do next.
pages.wider: The principle comes from CAST's Universal Design for Learning framework, with multiple means of action and expression, so that the method of responding doesn't decide who appears to understand.

why: Think, pair, share tends to fail in really predictable ways. There's no individual thinking before the talking starts, there are pairs where one voice does all the work, and there's a share stage answered by whoever volunteers. The disciplined version closes each of those gaps in turn.

Nomination carries the most weight. When any pupil might report back, the pair talk has to leave both partners able to answer, and the share becomes evidence about the room rather than a performance by the most confident voice.
example: In RE, pupils get one silent minute to note their own answer, two timed minutes to compare in pairs, and then the teacher names who reports back. Because nobody knew who would be chosen, both partners in each pair had a reason to make sure both of them could answer.
pages.try: Add the timer and the nomination to a think, pair, share you already use, and tell the class before the talk begins that you'll be choosing who shares, because it's that heads-up that gets everyone thinking rather than waiting.
notice: Whether the silent minute is actually silent. The individual think is the stage most often skipped, and it's the one the paired talk depends on.
What nominated pupils report back, whether it's their own view, their partner's, or a genuine combination of the two.
consider: A visible timer for the pair stage holds the structure in place without you having to police it.
Nominating kindly is a skill in itself, and how much warning a particular pupil needs before speaking to the room is a judgement for the teacher who knows them.
pages.wider: Wiliam's treatment of classroom talk keeps returning to the same move, which is structures that make evidence of thinking part of the routine rather than something volunteered.

why: Butler's finding is stark enough that the card leads with it: comments alone produced the greatest gains, and adding a grade to the comment cancelled it out. Given both, pupils read the grade, compare it with their neighbour's, and the comment might as well not be there at all.
When it comes to work in progress, removing the grades protects the only part of the marking that can still change the work.
example: A maths teacher returns a practice paper with comments identifying the strongest section and the step where marks were lost, and no score anywhere. The first ten minutes of the lesson go on acting on those comments, and scores only appear when the unit's final assessment arrives.
pages.try: Choose one piece of work in progress from one class and mark it comment only. Then watch what pupils do with the comments when there's no grade to look at first.
notice: Where pupils' eyes go when work comes back, and how many actually read past a grade when one is there.
Whether your comments give pupils something to do rather than something to feel.
consider: Work in progress is the card's boundary. Summative pieces still get graded, and the change protects feedback while the work can still improve.

Some marking policies expect grades on every piece, and how comment only marking sits with that expectation is a judgement for the teacher in the room, and sometimes a conversation in the department, rather than a rule a website can settle.
pages.wider: Butler compared grades, comments and the two combined. The gains sat with comments alone, and the combination did no better than grades by themselves.

why: The card sets a simple test: feedback must be more work for the recipient than the donor. Most written marking fails it, because a corrected error asks nothing of the pupil except to read it, or not, but a question about the error asks for an answer.
The card's other line is worth keeping whole: if feedback requires no response from the learner, it is not feedback; it is merely information.
example: Instead of correcting a misused apostrophe, a teacher writes: there are two apostrophe errors in this paragraph; find and fix both. The pupil then does the locating and the correcting, and that's where the thinking sits.
pages.try: In your next round of marking, try converting your five most common corrections into five reusable questions. The stock builds up quickly and it cuts the writing time too.
notice: Whether pupils actually respond, and in what depth. A question that gets ignored has caused no more thinking than a correction.
The ratio of your effort to theirs, page by page. The card's test is a blunt one, which makes it really easy to apply.
consider: Time for the response has to exist somewhere in a lesson. A question with no time set aside to answer it is just a correction with extra steps.
tech: An approved annotation tool with a reply function in your setting makes the response visible, because every question you leave either has an answer against it or it doesn't, for every pupil, and that record can shape what the next lesson revisits. The questions still have to be worth answering though, and the tool only shows you whether they were.
pages.wider: This is Wiliam's framing of feedback inside formative assessment: the purpose is to cause thinking that closes the gap, not to document errors.

why: Feedback given at the end of a unit, with nothing left to apply it to, is a record rather than an intervention. The card's fix is a structural one, so the next lesson begins with pupils reading and responding to their feedback before anything new arrives.
Those first few minutes are what make the marking you've already done worth the hours it took.
example: Books go back at the start of the lesson, and pupils spend the opening ten minutes on their responses, answering the questions left in the margins, redrafting one sentence, or correcting a method. New content waits until the responses are done.
pages.try: Protect the first ten minutes of one lesson this week for acting on feedback. Nothing else changes, and the feedback you were going to give anyway now has somewhere to land.
notice: What pupils do with the time without being prompted, which tells you how actionable the feedback actually was.
Whether the responses engage with the gap you identified. A tick and 'done' next to an unchanged answer is a response in name only.
consider: Sharing feedback in advance, where your school's systems allow it, means the lesson time starts at the responding rather than the reading.
If there's never time to act on it, the honest question is whether the feedback needed writing at all. The card puts it more bluntly: feedback with no time to act on it has no value.
pages.wider: Wiliam and Leahy treat time to act as part of the feedback itself rather than an optional follow-up, because feedback moves learning forward only while the work can still change.

why: Writing thirty individual comments takes hours, and each comment only ever helps one pupil. When it comes to reading the whole set for patterns though, not only is it much quicker, but you end up with something really useful for the whole class, because you can see what everyone did well, the errors that keep coming up, and two or three next steps that everyone can work on.
Teach to the gap, not to the individual paper, as the card has it, and the gaps repeat far more often than the papers do.
example: After reading a set of essays without writing on them, a teacher notes on a single page that conclusions were strong across the class, that evidence was rarely linked back to the question, and that three misconceptions kept coming up. The next lesson teaches the linking move to everyone, and then pupils go back to their own essays looking for it.
pages.try: Next marking session, read the whole set before writing anything. One page of patterns, and then decide what the following lesson is going to do about them.
notice: Whether the recurring errors actually recur less after being taught to, because that's the test of the next steps you chose.
Pupils who don't fit the patterns, in either direction. Whole class feedback still needs eyes on the outliers.
consider: The saving is in the writing, not the attention, and the patterns are only as good as the reading that finds them.
The card offers this as a way of keeping workload manageable, not a rule that no pupil ever gets an individual comment. Where individual response is still needed is your call.
pages.wider: It draws on Wiliam's case for evidence that changes the teaching, and on Hattie's finding that feedback helps most when it is specific about the next step in the work rather than about the person.

why: A correction does the cognitive work for the pupil and hopes some of it rubs off, but a question hands the work back. Returning a piece with three questions rather than a page of corrections keeps the effort where the card says it belongs: with the learner.
Three is a discipline as much as a number too, because choosing which three to ask forces you to decide which gaps really deserve the pupil's limited attention.
