example: On a science investigation write-up, instead of correcting the method section, the teacher writes: which variable did you actually change? How would a reader repeat step 3? What would make your conclusion safer? The pupil answers all three before starting the next investigation.
pages.try: Trial it on one set of books, with three questions, no corrections, and the requirement that the answers come before any new work. The requirement is the part that can't be skipped.
notice: The quality of the answers, because thin ones usually mean the question told the pupil what to write.
How long the questions take to write compared with your usual marking of the same work.
consider: The 'must respond before moving on' clause carries the whole strategy. Questions without protected time to answer them just collapse back into corrections that happen to have question marks.
pages.wider: The reasoning is Wiliam's: feedback should cause thinking, and correcting on the pupil's behalf takes away the struggle the learning depends on.

why: Between your model and independent work there's a gap, and pupils fall into it at really predictable points. Structured practice with peers, checked at every stage, puts a floor under that gap, so nobody moves on to step four carrying an unnoticed error from step two.
The card's first line sets the frame: independence is the destination, not the starting point.
example: Learning to balance chemical equations, pairs work through four equations one at a time, comparing answers after each one and sorting out any disagreements before the next. The teacher circulates listening out for pairs who agree on a wrong answer, because those are the errors that won't surface on their own.
pages.try: Take a practice set you already use and add one rule: check with your partner after every item, not at the end. That per-stage check is the difference between guided practice and marking each other's finished work.
notice: Pairs who agree quickly on wrong answers. Peer checking catches disagreement, but confident shared errors need you.
The point where the checking starts to slow down pupils who are ready to work alone. That's the signal to remove the structure rather than tighten it.
consider: The staging is doing the work here. A check at the end of a whole exercise arrives after the errors have compounded, and a check at every stage is what stops them compounding at all.
pages.wider: Guided practice with a high success rate before independent work is one of Rosenshine's principles of instruction, drawn from studies of what the most effective teachers actually do.

why: Answering a question exercises what a pupil knows, but writing one that could plausibly appear in an assessment asks for a lot more. They have to survey the topic, judge which ideas are assessable, and know the material well enough to say what a fair question and a correct answer look like. The card puts it directly: generating questions demands higher order thinking than simply answering them.
The questions come back to you as evidence too. What pupils choose to ask, and what they avoid, maps the topic as they see it.
example: Closing a unit on rivers, each pupil writes two possible assessment questions with answers. The teacher collates the strongest into next week's review quiz, and notices that almost nobody has written a question about deposition, which says something about where the class's confidence runs out.
pages.try: End one topic by asking pupils to write two questions that could be on the test, with answers, and then use the best of them in your next review.
notice: The level of the questions, whether they're pure recall or questions that need explanation and application to answer.
The topics nobody writes questions about, because avoidance is data too.
consider: A vague or unanswerable question usually points at a gap in understanding the content rather than the task, which makes it worth following up rather than discarding.
pages.wider: Black and Wiliam place this kind of activity with students as resources for, and owners of, their own learning: the assessment thinking starts to move from teacher to pupil.

why: Peer assessment has a bad name in classrooms where it just means swapping books and hunting for spelling errors. The card locates the fault precisely: without shared criteria, peer feedback is opinion, not evidence.

The structure starts before any assessing happens. Pupils who have looked at exemplars and agreed what quality looks like have a standard to assess against, but pupils who haven't can only compare the work with their own taste.
example: Before assessing each other's speeches, the class watches two recorded examples and agrees what separated them. Only then do pairs assess, against that agreed list, with one rule, which is that every judgement has to point to a specific moment in the speech.
pages.try: Before your next peer assessment, add in one exemplar discussion and have the class agree the criteria they'll use. Same task, just one added step.
notice: Whether the feedback cites the shared criteria or drifts back to personal preference.
How pupils receive peer judgements compared with yours, and whether criteria they helped build change that.
consider: Pairings carry social weight. Who assesses whom, and whether some work is better assessed anonymously, is exactly the kind of call the teacher in the room makes and a website can't.
pages.wider: Sadler's argument is that any assessor needs a concept of quality they can apply, and Berger's classroom practice shows pupils building that concept from real examples of excellent work.

why: Most quizzing looks at what was taught today or this week, which is really useful for checking the teaching worked, but it can't tell you whether pupils will still have that learning next month. That's where spaced retrieval comes in. As the card notes, returning to older material at increasing intervals is one of the most robust findings in memory research, and the idea at the heart of it is simple: coming back to something after you've had time to forget a little of it does far more for remembering than going over it again straight away.

The reason it sits with formative assessment is that the results tell you something you can use. If lots of the class have forgotten something, you know what needs revisiting, and you know in good time, before that knowledge is needed again.
example: A weekly low stakes quiz in history might have two questions from last week, two from the last unit, and one from all the way back in the autumn term. If the autumn question is the one most pupils get wrong, it goes back into the quiz in a different form the following week.
pages.try: Have a go by adding one deliberately old question to a quiz routine you already run. Even one question will start to show you what's faded, and you can build up from there.
notice: How pupils do on recent material compared with older material. It's completely normal for the older material to be weaker, and that difference is exactly what the spacing is there to help with.

How pupils react to getting the older questions wrong. For this to work they need to feel that a wrong answer is fine and just shows what needs another look, so it's worth keeping an eye on whether the low stakes genuinely feel low stakes to them.
consider: It can be tempting for pupils to prepare by re-reading their notes, and the card is explicit that re-reading notes is not the same as retrieving. Pupils will often default to re-reading because it feels easier, so it's worth being clear with them about the difference.

How far apart to space the returns is a professional judgement for the teacher in the room, made with this class and this content in front of them. The increasing intervals are the principle, but when the returns actually happen is up to you, because you know your class and your content better than any schedule written by someone else.
pages.wider: The thinking behind this comes from Bjork's work on desirable difficulties, which found that spacing and retrieval both make practice feel harder in the moment, but that this difficulty is a good sign, because it's doing the work that helps the learning stick for the longer term.

why: Putting questions to a class they can't yet be expected to answer looks pointless on the face of it, but the card's mechanism says otherwise. Triggering the feeling of not knowing primes attention for the explanation that follows, and pupils who struggle towards an answer before the instruction remember the real one better.

There's a second yield for the teacher too. The pre-quiz shows you what the class already knows, and which misconceptions are arriving with them, before you decide where the teaching needs its weight.
example: Before a unit on electricity, a short ungraded quiz asks pupils to predict what happens to bulbs in series and parallel circuits. The wrong predictions surface the familiar current-gets-used-up idea, and the first lesson is built to confront it.
pages.try: Open your next new topic with five questions pupils can't yet be expected to answer, framed exactly that way: you're not supposed to know this yet, so have a go anyway.
notice: How the same questions land after the teaching. The before-and-after pair gives you the clearest picture of what the unit added.
Whether the framing holds. If pupils experience the pre-quiz as a test, the low stakes are gone and so is the willingness to guess.
consider: The mechanism runs on struggle, so failing at the start has to be explicitly safe. That comes from how you introduce it and how you react to the wrong answers, not from the quiz itself.
pages.wider: Pre-testing belongs to Bjork's family of desirable difficulties, and Wiliam's interest is in the same activity read as evidence of where learners are before the teaching starts.

why: Asking a class whether they understand invites just about the least reliable answer in teaching. Asking each pupil, anonymously, what they're least clear about gets you the truth, because nobody has to own a confusion publicly.
Two minutes at the end of a lesson buys you the agenda for the start of the next one, drawn from the pupils' actual sticking points rather than your guess at them.
example: In the last two minutes, every pupil writes the one thing from today they're least sure about, with no names, and the slips go in a box on the way out. Three pupils name the same step in the method, so the next lesson opens by reteaching that step to everyone.
pages.try: Run it tomorrow with slips of paper or an anonymous form, whichever is less fuss. The only rule that really matters is that the most common muddy point gets addressed, publicly, next lesson.
notice: Clusters. One pupil's confusion is individual, but eight naming the same idea is a teaching point.
The pupils who write that nothing is muddy, every single time. Certainty that consistent deserves a careful check of its own.
consider: The loop has to close. If muddy points vanish into the box and never come back out, pupils stop telling you the truth within a fortnight.
Keep it anonymous. The honesty is the entire value of it, and it disappears the moment names go on slips.
pages.wider: The technique comes out of the classroom assessment tradition in higher education, and it survives in schools for the same reason, which is honest evidence at almost no cost.
tech: An anonymous response tool on your setting's approved list makes the collection easy and genuinely nameless, which protects the honesty this all depends on. Slips of paper in a box do the same job, so choose whichever your pupils will trust.

why: Rosenshine begins his principles with review for a good reason. In the classroom studies, the most effective teachers opened their lessons with it and checked understanding constantly, and a brief review of prior content, every lesson, keeps older learning warm and gives you a running read on what has stuck.

The card carries its own decision rule too: if most pupils cannot answer, adjust the pace of teaching. So the review is evidence collection with a consequence attached, rather than a settling activity.
example: Five questions go on the board as pupils arrive, two from yesterday, two from last week and one from last month. Answers go on paper, pupils check their own, and there's a show of results for each. When the last-month question is right in six books out of thirty, that topic goes back on next week's plan.
notice: Which time horizon fails first, whether it's yesterday's content, last week's or last month's.
Whether the results ever actually change your plan. A review that never alters the pace has become a ritual.
Which pupils only ever get caught out by the older material, and whether it's the same pupils every time.
consider: Little really does mean little. Ten minutes that grow into twenty crowd out the teaching the review is there to serve.
Keep the stakes low too. The information dries up as soon as the review starts to feel like a test.
pages.wider: The daily, weekly and monthly review pattern comes from Rosenshine's principles of instruction, distilled from observation of the most effective classrooms.

why: Re-reading notes feels productive because the material becomes familiar, and familiarity imitates knowing. Self quizzing feels worse and works better, and in the card's words, retrieval effort drives long term memory.
Teaching pupils to quiz themselves passes on the whole of this strand's machinery too. The checking that has been happening in your lessons becomes something they can run without you.
example: A teacher demonstrates a revision cycle: cover the notes, write everything you can recall about the topic, check against the notes, and mark the gaps as the material to come back to in a few days. Pupils practise the cycle in class, on content from a fortnight ago, before being asked to use it at home.
pages.try: Teach the cover, write, check cycle explicitly in one lesson. The moment where pupils check and find their gaps is the part to make visible, because that's the moment re-reading never gives them.
notice: Which pupils go back to re-reading when unsupervised. The pull of the easier strategy is strong precisely because it feels like progress.
Whether self quizzing turns up in how pupils talk about their revision, not just in the lesson where you taught it.
consider: The spaced part needs just as much teaching as the quizzing. Coming back to material after days rather than minutes is what the card's title is carrying, and it's the half pupils are most likely to drop.
pages.wider: Bjork's research underpins both halves of this card, retrieval as a desirable difficulty, and learners' unreliable instincts about which study strategies actually work.

why: You can spend hours marking and produce no feedback at all, because if a pupil never reads or acts on your comments, you've marked the work but nothing has actually been fed back. Without that engagement, there's simply no feedback.

The distinction really changes where the effort goes. Marking is finished when you put the pen down, but feedback isn't finished until the pupil has done something because of it, so the engagement has to be planned before the work goes back rather than hoped for afterwards.
example: A history teacher returning essays plans the first ten minutes of the next lesson before writing a single comment. Pupils will reread their feedback, rewrite one sentence in response, and be ready to say what their comment asked of them, which means the comments get written knowing exactly how they'll be used.
pages.try: Before you mark your next set, decide what pupils will do with the comments and when they'll do it. If you can't find that time, it's worth marking less and protecting it.
notice: Whether pupils read comments without being prompted, or wait to be told to.
How many of your comments actually lead to a visible change in the work.
How long the engagement takes compared with how long the marking took, because the gap can be really telling.
consider: Engagement needs lesson time, which means something else has to give way, and that trade-off is a planning decision rather than an afterthought.
A comment written for a pupil to act on reads differently from a comment written to show the work was marked, and it really helps to know which one you're writing.
tech: Audio comments and digital ink can shorten the gap between the work and your response to almost nothing, and feedback that arrives while the work is still fresh has a much better chance of shaping what pupils do next. The tool doesn't change the rule though, because a recorded comment nobody listens to is still marking rather than feedback. If you use the approved audio or annotation tool in your setting, plan the listening and the response with just as much care as the recording.
pages.wider: This sits squarely in Wiliam's account of formative assessment, where comments and evidence only count for anything once they change what the learner does next.

why: Most comments tell a pupil how they did and then stop there. Hattie and Timperley's three questions, where am I going, how am I doing, and what next, are a really quick test of whether a comment can actually move the work on.

A comment that only answers the second question leaves the pupil holding a judgement with nowhere to take it. The first question needs criteria that have been shared, and the third needs a next step the pupil can actually act on.
example: A science teacher marking investigation write-ups checks each comment against the three questions before handing the books back. Where a comment reads only as a verdict, she adds a line naming the goal and a line naming the next move, so a pupil might read: your conclusion describes the pattern, the criteria ask you to explain it, so use your graph to say why it happens.
pages.try: Take the last five comments you wrote and sort them against the three questions. If the middle column fills up fastest, you'll know what to add next time.
notice: Whether pupils can tell you, in their own words, what their next step is after reading your comment.
Which of the three questions your comments tend to favour when you look across a whole set.
consider: Where am I going only works when criteria have been shared and understood first, which is Sadler's territory as much as this card's.
What next needs time to act built in, otherwise the third question gets answered and then wasted.
pages.wider: Hattie and Timperley's review found feedback to be among the most powerful influences on achievement and among the most variable too, and the three questions are their account of what makes the difference.

why: Not all comments do the same job. Hattie and Timperley distinguish feedback aimed at the task, feedback aimed at the process the pupil used, and feedback aimed at the person, and the levels aren't equally useful, because task and process feedback improve learning while praise aimed at the self actually undermines it.

Naming your target before you write is a small habit that makes a really big difference to what ends up on the page, and a comment about the person is usually easy to spot once you start looking for it.
example: Marking a set of maths books, a teacher catches himself about to write that a pupil is a natural at this, and replaces it with a process comment instead: checking your answer against an estimate is what caught the error here. The warmth is just the same, but the target is different.
pages.try: For one class set, label each comment T, P or S as you write it, for task, process or self. The labels are for you rather than the pupils.
notice: How much of your praise, when you label it honestly, turns out to be aimed at the person.
Whether pupils can say what a comment was about, whether that's the answer, the method, or them.
consider: Warmth belongs in the classroom, it just shouldn't be doing the job of feedback on the learning, and the two can happily live in the same conversation without living in the same sentence.
pages.wider: The levels come from Hattie and Timperley's model of feedback, and their warning about self-level praise turns up independently too, in Kluger and DeNisi's findings on feedback that draws attention to the self.

why: Kluger and DeNisi's finding is one of the most sobering in this strand, because over a third of the feedback interventions they looked at actually made performance worse. Feedback is powerful, but the power runs in both directions.

The dividing line in their analysis is where the attention goes. Comments that keep a pupil's attention on the work tend to help, and comments that pull attention onto the self tend not to. The check on the card, work or student, is simply the practical version of that finding.
example: Before returning books, a languages teacher reads her own comments as if she were the pupil receiving them. Two turn out to be about the pupil rather than the translation in front of them, so both get rewritten to name something in the work, such as this tense is the one to fix, or these five words need the accent check you used above.
notice: How pupils respond in the moment work is returned, whether that's heads down into the work or looking around comparing themselves with others.
Which of your comments you'd be glad to receive about your own work.
consider: A comment can be about the student without ever naming them. Try harder, more effort needed and you can do better are all self-directed, whatever the phrasing.
pages.wider: As the strand's opening argument puts it, some feedback helps, some does very little, and some makes things worse, and Kluger and DeNisi supplied the numbers behind that sentence.

why: Before feedback can do anything, three conditions have to hold. Sadler's argument, which anchors so much of this strand, is that pupils must know what quality looks like, be able to compare their own work against it, and have the chance to close the gap they find.

Miss any one of them and the rest stalls. Criteria shared after the work is finished can't guide it, a comparison pupils can't make wastes the criteria, and a gap identified with no time to close it just sits there.
example: Before a design and technology project begins, the class looks at the criteria alongside two finished products of different quality and talks about which criteria separate them. Halfway through making, pupils stop and place their own work against the same criteria before deciding what to do next.
pages.try: Check one upcoming task against the three conditions, so criteria shared first, a built-in moment to compare, and time to act on what the comparison shows. Add whichever one is missing before changing anything else.
notice: Whether pupils' judgements of their own work start to look more like yours, which is the comparison condition beginning to work.
Which of the three conditions your current routine handles least well, because there's usually one.
consider: Criteria pupils have never seen exemplified tend to stay abstract, and showing what quality looks like in real work can do more than a list of statements on its own.
The three conditions are a design test as much as a marking one, so they can be checked before a task is set and not just afterwards.
pages.wider: Sadler's conditions are the hinge of this whole strand, and Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick built directly on them, placing feedback within pupils' growing ability to judge and improve their own work.

why: Some errors really shouldn't be left to sit. On simple and procedural tasks, Shute found that quick feedback stops mistakes embedding, because every repetition of a wrong method is practice at being wrong.
Waiting until next lesson to fix something that could be fixed now gives the error a whole week of rehearsal.
example: During column subtraction practice, a teacher checks answers as pupils work rather than collecting the books in. A pupil subtracting the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position gets caught on question three rather than question thirty.
pages.try: Pick one procedural practice task this week and mark it live, in the room, instead of taking it away. Books stay open and errors get fixed at the desk.
notice: Whether the same procedural errors come back later in the week, which is the real test of whether the correction landed.
What pupils do immediately after a correction, whether they redo the question or move straight on.
consider: Immediate correction is for the simple and procedural. On complex work the guide's advice runs the other way, which is to let the struggle do its work first.
Deciding which tasks count as simple is a judgement about your class and your subject, and the teacher in the room knows that far better than a website does.
tech: An approved auto-marked quiz or response tool in your setting can give every pupil that immediate correction all at once, which no teacher circulating a room can match for procedural practice. The trap named in this strand still applies though, because a score, a tick or a badge that stops there is information, not feedback. Build in the moment where pupils redo the questions they got wrong, or all that speed achieves nothing.
pages.wider: Shute's review of formative feedback is the source here, and her point is that timing isn't a matter of taste but of task, with quick correction suited to simple work.

why: Speed isn't always a virtue. On complex work, the research Shute and Kulhavy report points to a short delay before feedback, because immediate correction can short-circuit the very thinking the task was set to provoke.
A pupil midway through wrestling with a hard problem doesn't need the answer arriving, they need the wrestle, and feedback that lands too early can turn a thinking task into a copying one.
example: After pupils attempt a multi-step physics problem, the teacher collects the attempts in and says nothing that lesson. The feedback comes at the start of the next one, once pupils have a bit of distance from their own reasoning, and it begins by asking them to name their sticking point before they read the comment.
pages.try: Choose one genuinely complex task and deliberately hold your feedback back for a day, and notice what you would have interrupted.
notice: Whether pupils persist for longer when they know correction isn't imminent.
What pupils ask you during the task when they can't hand the struggle straight back to you.
consider: This card and Immediate for Simple Tasks are really one principle rather than two, which is to match the timing to the complexity of the task, and which is which is a judgement for the teacher who knows the class and the content.
Delay means short here. A day or a lesson lets the processing happen, but two weeks is just slow marking.
pages.wider: Shute's review and Kulhavy's earlier work both found that feedback timing interacts with task difficulty, so there's no single right speed, only a right speed for this task.

why: Feedback returned weeks after the work is a bit of a post-mortem, accurate perhaps, but too late to change anything. Feedback given while pupils are still working shapes the work itself, which is the formative case Black and Wiliam made.
There's a lot to be said for proximity too. Moving around the room during the task puts you exactly where feedback is cheapest and most usable, at the point of the error and in the moment it happens.
example: While pupils draft persuasive letters, the teacher circulates on a deliberate route rather than answering hands. Reading over shoulders, she catches the same weak opening in four books and pauses the room for ninety seconds to deal with it before it spreads any further.
pages.try: In your next extended task, plan your route around the room the way you'd plan a question, so you know who you'll reach first and what you're looking for when you arrive.
notice: How many errors you catch mid-task that would otherwise have travelled home with you in thirty books.
Which pupils you naturally reach and which you consistently miss, because a deliberate route usually shows up a pattern.
consider: Stepping in during the moment suits some errors and not others, and on complex thinking the guide advises letting the struggle run first, so in-the-moment feedback is a timing choice rather than a default.
pages.wider: This is Black and Wiliam's central argument in practical form, which is that assessment is only formative when it adjusts teaching and learning while the learning is still underway.

why: Butler's study gives this strand one of its clearest warnings. When a grade sits alongside a comment, pupils look at the grade and miss the guidance, and it was comments alone that produced the greatest gains.
The grade doesn't just distract from the comment, it cancels it, and two lines of careful writing in the margin simply can't compete with a number at the top of the page.
example: A geography teacher returns assessed work with comments only. Pupils respond to the comments and improve one section, and only then, at the end of the week, do the grades go into the gradebook and become visible.
pages.try: Choose one low-stakes piece and return it comment-only, then compare what pupils do with it against what they did last time a grade was attached.
notice: The first thing pupils look for when work comes back, and how long they spend on the words once there's no number to find.
Whether the talk between pupils starts to shift from comparing scores to comparing responses.
consider: If your school mandates grades, the card's advice is about sequencing rather than defiance, so delay the grade until the feedback has been used.
Comment-only work still needs comments worth acting on, and taking the grade away really exposes the quality of what's left.
tech: Most digital gradebooks and annotation tools show pupils a score the moment work is returned, which puts Butler's problem straight back on the screen. If the approved tool in your setting has a hide-grades or scheduled-release option, it's well worth using, so pupils get the comments first, then time to respond, and the number afterwards.
pages.wider: Butler's research distinguished task-involving from ego-involving feedback, and a grade pulls attention towards how I did as a person, which is precisely the attention shift Kluger and DeNisi found so costly.

why: A page of comments overwhelms the pupil and exhausts the teacher, and lots of it goes unread anyway. The evidence in this guide is blunt about that: feedback is not what the teacher gives, it is what the learner does with it, and nobody does thirty things with thirty comments.
One or two precise targets land. Choosing them is actually harder than writing many, because it forces you to make a judgement about what would make the biggest difference to this pupil right now.
example: Marking a set of essays, a teacher writes one sentence per script, which is the single change that would most improve the next draft. The marking gets noticeably quicker, but the real change comes next lesson, when pupils spend ten minutes acting on the target and for once every pupil knows exactly what theirs is.
pages.try: Mark your next class set with a one-target rule. If you catch yourself writing a second comment, ask whether it's more important than the first, and if it is, swap them over.
notice: Whether pupils can tell you their target the next day. With a page of comments they usually can't, but with one they usually can.
What happens to the quality of the targets you choose when the choosing is the whole job.
consider: Less volume only works alongside time to act, so one precise target that pupils never get a lesson minute to work on is still wasted effort.
This is about work in progress, and summative points where fuller commentary is required are a different job altogether.
pages.wider: Kluger and DeNisi's meta-analysis found over a third of feedback interventions made performance worse, and precision and focus are a big part of what separates the feedback that helps.
tech: A digital highlight or pin tool, the approved one in your setting, suits this really well, because you get one marked spot and one comment with nothing else competing for attention. Audio comments can carry the single target quickly too, but faster feedback only counts for anything if pupils actually use it.

why: Handing assessment over to pupils without structure produces exactly what Topping's research predicts, so you get empty praise, vague niceness and the occasional unkindness. With criteria and a protocol though, peer feedback becomes learning for both the giver and the receiver.
There's a second benefit hiding in it too. Judging another pupil's work against criteria is practice at the very comparison Sadler says pupils must learn to make about their own.
example: Pupils swap lab reports with a fixed protocol. They check the report against two named criteria, mark where each one is met, and write one question for the author, with no general comments allowed. The teacher then samples the peer feedback itself, because the quality of the judging is evidence too.
pages.try: Start with one criterion rather than a rubric. Pupils check a partner's work against a single shared criterion and mark exactly where it is or isn't met.
notice: The language pupils use about work, because criteria words appearing in their talk is the structure doing its job.
Whether the feedback stays on the work or drifts to the person, which pupils find just as hard as adults do.
consider: The protocol carries the strategy, and without it the activity tends to slide back to swap-and-be-nice within a lesson or two.
Pupils need feedback literacy before they can give feedback, not just receive it, so modelling what a useful peer comment looks like is worth doing at least once first.
pages.wider: Topping's work on peer assessment found benefits flowing to the assessor and the assessed alike, provided the structure holds, and the structure isn't an optional extra, it's the part that makes the whole thing work.

why: Andrade's finding rearranges the usual worry about self-assessment. Pupils' judgements don't need to be accurate for the practice to work, because it's the act of comparing work against criteria that improves performance, so the process really is the point.

That takes a lot of the pressure off. You're not training examiners, you're giving pupils repeated practice at holding their work up against a standard, which is exactly the comparison Sadler's conditions require.
example: Before handing in an essay, pupils complete a short self-review against the criteria, saying where each one is met, where it isn't, and one change they've made as a result. The teacher marks the essay afterwards as usual, but reads the self-review first.
pages.try: Add one line to your submission routine, which is to ask pupils to mark the place where they best meet the criteria and the place where they least do, before the work comes to you.
notice: Whether pupils' self-judgements move closer to yours over a term. Accuracy isn't the goal, but drift towards it suggests the comparing is genuine.
What pupils change between the self-review and submission, because a self-assessment that changes nothing was really just a form-filling exercise.
consider: Self-assessment against criteria pupils don't understand is guesswork, so Sadler's first condition, knowing what quality looks like, comes before this card rather than after it.
pages.wider: Andrade's research sits within the same self-regulation tradition as Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick and Boud, which is feedback practice that builds the pupil's own evaluative judgement rather than just improving the next piece of work.

why: A written comment is usually a full stop. Carless's research argues for making it a turn in a conversation instead, so pupils question, clarify and respond to comments over time rather than receiving a final judgement.

Uptake really does rise when feedback works this way, partly because a pupil who can ask what a comment means no longer has to guess, and a pupil who has replied to a comment has already begun to act on it.
example: A teacher returns draft coursework with two margin comments each, one of them ending in a question. Pupils reply in writing before redrafting, and the teacher answers the replies rather than writing fresh comments, so each piece carries a short thread of exchange rather than a verdict.
pages.try: End one comment per pupil with a question that needs an answer, and collect the answers in. The replies will show you which comments were understood.
notice: Which comments get genuine replies and which get token ones, because the difference maps really closely onto which comments were worth writing.
Whether pupils start initiating, because asking about a comment is feedback literacy showing itself.
consider: Dialogue takes longer than delivery, so it can't be every piece. Choosing where a feedback conversation pays its way, usually a draft heading for redraft rather than a finished piece, is the design decision.
pages.wider: Carless's work on feedback uptake, alongside Boud's on learner capacity, points the same way, which is that pupils act on feedback they've had a hand in making sense of.

why: Not every kind of feedback needs you. Automated tools can check factual accuracy and procedural correctness faster than any teacher can, but what they can't do is respond to voice, argument or creativity. The card's advice is a division of labour, so you match the feedback source to what's being assessed.
Done well, this buys back the scarcest resource in the system, which is teacher attention, and spends it where automation simply can't go.
example: In a languages classroom, the approved practice tool handles vocabulary and conjugation accuracy, correcting as pupils go. The teacher's written feedback on the same unit leaves those layers alone and looks instead at how convincingly the pupil's letter argues its case.
pages.try: List what you marked in your last set, then sort it into accuracy and correctness on one side and voice, argument and quality of thinking on the other, and ask what on the first list a tool in your setting could carry for you.
notice: Whether your own comments become fewer and more substantial once the accuracy checking moves elsewhere.
Whether pupils act on automated corrections or just click past them, because a tick accepted without a redo has fed nothing back.
consider: The strand's warning applies with full force here: automated feedback that gives a score, a tick or a badge and stops there is information, not feedback. The tool supplies the correction, but you still supply the time and the expectation that pupils use it.
tech: The safest way to use this one is to stay with the card's own framing. Use the approved adaptive or AI-assisted tool in your setting for what it's designed to assess, which is factual accuracy and procedural correctness, and keep yourself for the rest, because judgements about argument, voice and creativity stay with you. The question to keep asking isn't whether the tool's feedback is fast, which it will be, but whether pupils do anything with it, and speed only counts when it leads to a correction, a retry or a redraft.
pages.wider: Shute's review supports quick, automated correction for procedural work, while Black and Wiliam's account of formative practice describes the thing no tool replaces, which is the professional judgement about where the learning goes next.

why: Reading a class set shows you things no single script can, such as the same misconception in eleven books, a strength half the class shares, or one gap that would repay some whole-class teaching. Whole class feedback works from those patterns, so you teach to the gap, not to each paper.

It's sustainable for you and precise for pupils, which is a rare combination in feedback, and thirty individual paragraphs saying the same thing serve nobody better than one well-taught response to the pattern.
example: After reading a set of essays without writing in them, a teacher notes three recurring issues and one common strength. The next lesson opens with the pattern, which covers what this class does well, the error many of them share, and the one improvement to make now, and pupils then find and fix that issue in their own work.
pages.try: Read your next set with a blank sheet beside you and nothing in your pen for the books. Record the patterns only, and build the follow-up lesson from the sheet.
notice: Whether pupils can find the general point in their own work, which is the step where whole class feedback succeeds or fails.
How your reading changes when you're hunting for patterns rather than composing comments.
consider: Some pupils will need the bridge built for them, because the class-level point and their own page aren't automatically connected, so a quick check on who has found their own example is well worth the two minutes.
Whole class feedback replaces some individual marking rather than all of it, and which pieces still need an individual response is a judgement about the work and the class.
tech: A shared display or class document is where the patterns become teachable, with the common strengths and errors laid out once, visible to everyone, and annotated live as the class works through them. Kept in the approved shared space in your setting, the same document becomes a running record of what this class has been taught to fix, which is really useful the next time a pattern threatens to come back.
pages.wider: This is Wiliam's formative logic applied at class scale, and it reflects Hattie and Timperley's point that feedback informs the teacher as much as the taught, because the set tells you what to do next.

why: The fastest way to make feedback backfire is to aim it at the person. Kluger and DeNisi found that comments which threaten self-concept decrease performance, because attention pulled to the self is attention pulled off the work.
The card's two examples carry the rule. This paragraph needs restructuring gives the pupil somewhere to go, but you need to try harder gives them somewhere to hide.
example: Rereading his comments before returning books, a teacher rewrites each one whose subject is the pupil until its subject is the work, so you have not explained this becomes this step needs the reason it works, and you must check your work becomes three of these answers fail the estimate test.
pages.try: Scan your last set of comments for sentences whose subject is the pupil, and rewrite each one so the subject is a specific piece of the work.
notice: Whether returned work produces defensiveness or redrafting, because the difference often follows where the comments were aimed.
Which pupils you most often address person-first, because it may well be exactly the ones for whom work-directed comments would help most.
consider: Task-directed doesn't mean cold, and the warmth can live in the conversation while the written feedback stays on the work.
pages.wider: Kluger and DeNisi's analysis holds that the closer feedback moves to the self, the less useful it becomes, and Hattie and Timperley's levels tell the same story from a different dataset.

why: If a comment asks nothing of the pupil, it's information rather than feedback. Wiliam's test is a demanding one, because the measure of feedback is the thinking it causes, and a comment that does the pupil's thinking for them causes none.
Why might this be stronger with evidence leaves work for the learner to do, but inserting the evidence yourself finishes the job and ends the learning.
example: A computing teacher stops writing the fix beside broken code. Instead each comment names the symptom and asks a question, such as this loop never ends, so what condition would stop it? Pupils write the answer down, and then they make the change.
pages.try: Before returning your next set, reread each comment and ask yourself what the pupil will have to think about to use it. If the answer is nothing, rewrite it.
notice: How long pupils spend with returned work, because comments that cause thinking take visible time to act on.
The quality of what pupils produce in response, because a poor response often points to a comment that told rather than asked.
consider: Causing thinking presupposes time to think, so this card falls flat without lesson minutes set aside for the response.
Not every comment needs to be a puzzle. Simple procedural slips are better corrected than pondered, so save the thinking for where the thinking pays.
pages.wider: This is Wiliam's contribution to the strand in a nutshell, which is that feedback exists to change the learner's thinking, and anything that bypasses the thinking bypasses the learning.

why: Praise feels safe, and that's exactly why it needs some care. Butler found that task-involving feedback improves performance while ego-involving feedback shifts attention from the learning to the self-image, and praise of traits, such as cleverness, talent or being a natural, is ego-involving however kindly it's meant.
Praise the strategy and the praise becomes reusable, because a pupil told their method worked can use that method again, but a pupil told they're gifted has nothing to act on.
example: A music teacher watching a pupil finally manage a difficult passage says: slowing it right down and only speeding up when it was clean, that is what got you there. The praise names something the pupil chose to do and can choose to do again.
pages.try: For a week, make every piece of praise name a decision the pupil made, and if you can't find the decision, watch a little longer before praising.
notice: Whether praised strategies get reused, both by the pupil praised and by those listening in.
What happens to pupils' willingness to have a go at hard tasks when praise attaches to methods rather than ability.
consider: This is a phrasing habit more than a policy, and habits shift slowly, so a short list of strategy-praise stems kept where you can see it, for you rather than the pupils, does a lot of the early lifting.
pages.wider: Butler's task- and ego-involvement distinction converges with Kluger and DeNisi's meta-analysis, because feedback that turns attention to the self, praise included, tends to cost performance rather than raise it.

why: Pupils are rarely taught how to read feedback, and it really shows. A comment that seems perfectly clear to the teacher who wrote it can be opaque to the pupil holding it, and acting on feedback is a skill with steps, because you have to understand the comment, find where it applies in the work, and know the move it's asking for.
Carless and Boud call this feedback literacy, and their point is right there on the card: it is taught, not assumed.
example: Before returning the first marked piece of the year, a teacher puts one of her own typical comments on the board and walks through it, showing what it says, what it means, and what she would do in response. Pupils then decode one of their own comments in pairs before having a go alone.
pages.try: Take the card's own script into your next return-of-work lesson, so one comment, modelled aloud, with the meaning and the next move included, before pupils touch their own.
notice: The questions pupils ask about comments, because fewer what-does-this-mean questions over a term is the literacy building.
Whether the modelling transfers, so can pupils decode a comment shaped differently from the one you modelled?
consider: Literacy is easier to build when there's a consistent shape to read. If your comments follow a predictable pattern, pupils can learn that pattern, but comments written differently every time keep them beginners.
pages.wider: Feedback literacy is Carless and Boud's term for the learner's side of the exchange, which is the capacity to understand, evaluate and use what comes back, and without it the teacher's side achieves very little.

why: Sometimes the most useful move is an audit rather than a new strategy. Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's seven principles give you the checklist, so do you clarify criteria, enable self-assessment, encourage dialogue and help close the gap? The card's instruction is a direct one: redesign where you do not.

The card names four of the principles as its worked examples, but the full seven are worth having to hand for the audit. Good feedback practice clarifies what good performance looks like, develops self-assessment and reflection, delivers high quality information to pupils about their learning, encourages dialogue around learning with teachers and peers, encourages positive motivational beliefs, provides opportunities to close the gap between current and desired performance, and gives teachers information they can use to shape their teaching.

Their deeper argument, which gets picked up throughout this strand, is that feedback belongs inside self-regulation, and its job is to make pupils better at judging and improving their own work rather than more dependent on yours.
example: A teacher audits one unit against the principles and finds two things missing, because pupils never self-assess before submitting and no comment ever gets a reply. She changes only those two things for the next unit and leaves what already works alone.
notice: Which principles your practice already covers without you ever having named them, and which are missing entirely.
Whether the redesigns hold once the unit is underway, or fall away under time pressure, because what falls first shows you what needs protecting.
consider: Trying to audit everything at once tends to change nothing, so one unit looked at honestly will do far more than a whole curriculum skimmed.
pages.wider: Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick built on Sadler's foundations, reframing feedback around the pupil's growing power of self-regulation, and the seven principles are that argument in a form you can actually use.

why: Time to act is the part that gets squeezed out most often, and the strand is blunt about the cost: feedback with no time to act on it is wasted. Every hour you spend marking either pays off or gets lost in the ten minutes after the work goes back.

Beginning the next lesson with pupils reading and responding to comments before anything new makes the priority structural rather than something you just hope for, because the response is the learning event and the comments were only ever the preparation for it.
example: Work goes back at the start of the lesson rather than the end. Pupils read their comments, rewrite one section in response, and only then does new content begin. There's nothing complicated about the routine, and its value is simply that it happens every time work is returned.
pages.try: Protect the first ten minutes after any returned work for responding to it, and put it in your planning as a fixed cost of setting the work in the first place.
notice: What pupils produce in the response window, because the redrafts are better evidence of your feedback's quality than the comments themselves.
Whether pupils begin expecting the routine and arrive ready to respond, which is the habit forming.
consider: If there's genuinely no time for pupils to act, the honest options are to mark less or to reclaim the time, because writing comments that will never be used is the one option the evidence rules out.
tech: Sharing feedback through the approved platform in your setting the evening before, as the card suggests, moves the reading out of the lesson so that the lesson time goes entirely on the response. The strand's closing line is the test to hold onto: the win is not faster feedback, the win is better work because pupils had time to use it.
pages.wider: Wiliam and Leahy's practical work on embedding formative assessment treats the response to feedback as a planned classroom routine rather than a hope, and this card is that principle in its simplest form.

why: When you correct a pupil's work for them, you do the thinking and they watch you do it. Returning work with questions instead keeps the cognitive work where the learning is, which is with the pupil.
What evidence supports this claim? asks something of the writer that inserting the missing evidence never will, and if feedback requires no response from the learner, it is information, not feedback.
example: An English teacher returns paragraphs with one margin question each, such as which word here tells the reader how to feel, or what is your evidence for this? The lesson opens with pupils answering their question in a different colour before any new content begins.
pages.try: On the next piece you mark, swap the corrections on one section for questions, and give five minutes next lesson for written answers. The answers will tell you whether the questions were any good.
notice: The quality of pupils' responses, because a question that gets a one-word answer back was probably just a correction with a question mark on the end.
Whether the same question stops being needed over time, which is the whole point of asking rather than fixing.
consider: Simple procedural slips are often better corrected straight away, and the guide is clear that quick feedback stops mistakes embedding on simple tasks, so save the questions for the thinking rather than the typos.
Pupils need to know how to act on a question, which is feedback literacy, and it has to be taught with an exemplar at least once.
pages.wider: This is Hattie and Timperley's territory, because feedback that works answers where next, and a good question is often the most honest form that answer can take.
tech: An annotation tool with a reply function, through your setting's approved platform, turns each margin question into a visible exchange, with your question and their written answer in one place. The reply is the point, because a question with nowhere to answer it is really just a correction in disguise.

why: Boud's argument reaches past the next piece of work. If pupils always need you to tell them how they did, the system has failed, however good the telling, because feedback should be building the learner's capacity to judge quality for themselves.

That reframes the goal of much of this strand. Criteria, self-assessment, dialogue and time to act aren't only ways to improve this essay, they're an apprenticeship in judging quality, and an apprenticeship is supposed to come to an end.
example: Across a term, pupils build a portfolio in which every submitted piece carries their own prior judgement against the criteria. The teacher's response engages with the judgement as much as the work, so where the pupil's assessment was sound it says so and steps back, and where it missed, that gap becomes the feedback.
pages.try: Before your next round of marking, ask pupils to predict the feedback they'll get. Your marking then confirms, refines or corrects their judgement, which is exactly the capacity you're trying to build.
notice: Whether pupils' predictions of their feedback sharpen up over time.
Who still can't start work without asking whether it's right, and whether that number falls.
consider: Independence is designed in gradually rather than declared. The scaffolds of criteria and structured self-review come first and fade later, and how fast to fade them is a judgement about the class in front of you.
pages.wider: Boud's case for sustainable feedback takes Sadler's conditions and Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's self-regulation principles to their logical end, which is feedback that gradually makes itself unnecessary.

why: Good feedback rarely happens by accident, and the closing card of the strand says why: feedback designed into learning from the start works, and left to chance, it doesn't. Who gives it, when it comes, what form it takes and when pupils act on it are all scheme-of-work decisions rather than things you improvise on marking night.

Designing it in also makes the rest of the strand affordable, because comment-only pieces, peer review, whole class feedback and response time stop competing for lesson minutes when the scheme already holds a place for each of them.
example: Planning a six-week unit, a teacher fixes two feedback points before sequencing any content, so a mid-unit draft that gets whole class feedback with a response lesson, and a final piece that gets individual comments with time to act. Everything else in the unit is arranged around those fixed points.
pages.try: Open your next unit plan and look for the moment pupils act on feedback. If you can't point to it, add it before you add anything else.
notice: How the designed feedback points survive contact with the term, because what gets skipped under pressure shows you where the design needs protecting, or rethinking.
Whether pupils know the rhythm, so when feedback is coming and what they'll be expected to do with it.
consider: Design includes deciding what won't get detailed feedback, because a scheme that promises rich feedback on everything is unlikely to deliver it on anything.
pages.wider: Sadler's conditions, Carless's dialogue and Boud's sustainability all describe systems rather than moments, and this card draws the conclusion, which is that feedback is a feature of curriculum design rather than an event that follows it.

why: Anderson and Krathwohl give you a really useful map of what a question is asking a learner to do, whether that's remembering, understanding, applying, analysing, evaluating or creating. Without a map like this, questioning tends to settle into one register, and the talk in your classroom can end up much thinner than the thinking you're actually after.

The card's caution is just as important as the taxonomy itself, which is that these are not a hierarchy of worth. Recall is foundational, not inferior, and a lesson full of analysis questions built on insecure knowledge doesn't really help anybody.
example: Imagine a history teacher looking back across a fortnight of questions on the causes of the First World War. Asking what year or which countries is remembering. Asking why the alliance system raised the stakes is analysing. Asking whether any single country was most responsible is evaluating. Nothing about the teaching has changed yet, but the teacher can now see which kinds of thinking are being asked for and which ones never get a look in.
pages.try: Write down the questions you asked in one lesson, from memory or from your slides, and place each one against the six levels. The spread you find, or the lack of it, is the useful bit.
notice: Which levels come up again and again across a week, and which never appear at all.
Whether your recall questions are doing their foundational work before you ask for analysis or evaluation.
What happens to the answers when you deliberately ask at a level you rarely use.
consider: The taxonomy is a map rather than a ladder to be climbed in every lesson. Which level a class needs next is a judgement about their knowledge, and that judgement is yours to make.
It pairs really naturally with planning questions before the lesson, because the levels are most useful before the room fills up.
pages.wider: Anderson and Krathwohl's revision of the taxonomy is one of the most widely used frameworks for question design, and their insistence that recall is foundational, not inferior, is the part that gets forgotten most often.

why: Not every good question suits every moment, and Hattie and Zierer make a really helpful distinction here. Surface questions establish what, deep questions probe why, and transfer questions ask where else this applies, and each one serves a different stage of learning.

The thing that tends to go wrong is reaching for transfer too early. If you ask students to apply a concept elsewhere before the surface knowledge is secure, you're setting them up to fail, and that failure can look like inability when it's really just sequencing.
example: Early in a unit on electricity you might ask what the components of this circuit are. Once that's secure, you can ask why the bulb dims when a second one is added. Later still, you can ask where else the idea of sharing a limited supply turns up. It's the same topic all the way through, but three stages and three different kinds of question.
pages.try: Before writing the key questions for your next lesson, ask yourself one question first, which is what stage this class is at with this content.
notice: How students handle why questions, because struggle there often tells you the surface layer isn't secure yet.
Whether the discussion changes when the question matches the stage the class is at rather than the ambitions of the scheme of work.
consider: Stage is about this class and this content right now, not about ability. The same lesson can hold students at different stages, and only you can see where each one is.
Surface questions aren't lesser questions. The previous card makes the same point about recall, and the two frameworks agree with each other.
pages.wider: The surface, deep and transfer model comes from Hattie and Zierer's synthesis of how learning moves through phases, and each phase has its own kind of question.

why: Most classroom questions have a destination the teacher already holds, and students know it. Dillon found that genuine open questions, the ones where the teacher really doesn't know the answer, produce the most extended student reasoning.
That's a different thing from a closed question dressed up in open clothing. Guess what I'm thinking is a game rather than an enquiry, and students play it efficiently rather than thoughtfully.
example: An English teacher asks which character in the novel changes most, and she genuinely hasn't decided herself. Students take different positions, and because there's no answer to converge on, they have to argue from the text. The discussion runs longer than planned and doesn't resolve, and that's fine.
pages.try: Plan one genuinely open question into next week, one where you'd find it hard to say what a right answer would even look like.
notice: The length of the reasoning compared with your closed questions, which is exactly what Dillon measured.
Whether students start addressing each other rather than routing everything through you.
Your own urge to steer the room towards a view you privately hold.
consider: Not every question needs a predetermined destination, but lots of them still will. Open questions do their work partly because they're occasional and genuine rather than the default.
An open question still needs something to reason with, so a class without secure knowledge of the novel can't really argue about it.
tech: A shared whiteboard or discussion board from your school's approved set can hold the range of positions an open question produces, and it keeps the reasoning there to come back to in a later lesson, so a really useful conversation isn't lost the moment the lesson moves on. It can also bring in students who wouldn't venture an unfinished idea out loud, though the thinking still has to be theirs.
pages.wider: Dillon's studies of questioning are unusual for how sceptical they are about questions themselves, and this card and its neighbour on alternatives both come out of that scepticism.

why: Questions asked on the spur of the moment tend to default to recall, and the card is precise about why: not because recall is wrong but because planning stops there. In the flow of a lesson, the question that comes to mind is simply the one that's easiest to form.
Writing your questions before the lesson, at every level of Anderson and Krathwohl's taxonomy, is what turns the framework from a poster on the wall into a genuinely useful planning tool.
example: Planning a lesson on rivers, a geography teacher writes six questions into the slides in advance, from what is erosion right through to how would you defend this village, and why there. In the lesson the questions are simply ready and waiting, instead of needing to be invented in the middle of an explanation.
pages.try: For one lesson this week, write three questions in advance at levels you know you wouldn't improvise, and put them somewhere you'll actually see them.
notice: The difference in students' answers between your planned questions and your improvised ones.
Which of your planned questions you actually asked, because the ones that never got used tell you something about the shape of the lesson.
consider: Plan the pivotal questions rather than a script. The point is to have the harder questions ready, not to close down where the discussion goes.
Improvised questions keep their place too, because responsiveness is part of the craft. Planning removes the ceiling, it doesn't remove the improvising.

stair.lede: Drafting a ladder of questions across the levels is planning work AI can really help to speed up, through the approved tool in your setting, with the framework the card names built into the prompt:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary English teacher. Create a set of questions on the poem I am teaching to Year 10, one question at each of these levels: remembering, understanding, applying, analysing, evaluating, creating.

Label each question with its level. Keep every question concise and answerable in discussion, not as an essay task.

Do not include answers, model responses or commentary.

[paste the poem or topic details here]
stair.after: The levels are a planning tool rather than a hierarchy of worth, and recall is foundational, not inferior. Draft with the tool, then choose and reorder for your class, and keep iterating until the ladder fits the lesson you're actually teaching.

pages.wider: This is Anderson and Krathwohl put to work, with the taxonomy read not so much as a description of questions, but as a discipline for writing them.
tech: A lesson planning or slide tool keeps your planned questions where you'll actually use them. The planning is the strategy, and the tool simply stores it.

why: Dillon's finding runs against instinct, because statements and silence often draw out richer responses than questions do. A steady stream of questions can turn a discussion into an interrogation, with the teacher's voice doing all the driving and every exchange routed through the front.

Saying tell me more, or I had not considered that, hands the floor back without demanding a particular answer, and the card's own summary is the one to remember: not every probe needs to end with a question mark.
example: Picture a discussion of a moral question in RE, where a pupil offers a view. The teacher simply says, I had not considered that, and stops there. The pupil keeps going, and then a second pupil responds to the first one rather than waiting for the next question to arrive.
notice: What comes after a statement compared with what comes after a question.
How many questions you ask in ten minutes of discussion, because just counting them is revealing in itself.
Whether pupils start responding to each other when you probe less.
consider: Silence is one of Dillon's alternatives too, which makes wait time the natural companion to this card.
Statements only really work when they're genuine, so I had not considered that only lands if you actually hadn't.
pages.wider: Dillon spent a career questioning whether questions deserve their central place in classroom talk, and his alternatives are the practical result of all that work.

why: Mary Budd Rowe timed teachers waiting after their questions and found that most give less than a second before speaking again, whether that's rephrasing, prompting or answering the question themselves. Under a second isn't thinking time for anyone.

Extending the pause to three seconds costs nothing, needs no resources, and it changes the answers you get. The silence after a question isn't dead air, it's often where the better thinking gets started.
example: A teacher asks why the character makes the choice she does, and then counts to three in their head. The silence feels far longer from the front than it does from the desks. The first answer that comes is a sentence rather than a single word, and a second pupil builds on it without being prompted.
pages.try: Pick one lesson and hold three seconds after every substantive question. Counting silently isn't a gimmick, because the urge to fill the gap is strong enough that you really do need a mechanism.
notice: The length and complexity of the answers, which is exactly what Rowe measured improving.
Who answers. The extra seconds bring in pupils who like to compose their answer before speaking and were always beaten to it before.
Your own discomfort, which fades with practice, and it's a small price for the better answers.
consider: The pause after a pupil answers matters too, and it's a strategy in its own right, so the pair of them are stronger together.
Three seconds of silence only helps in a room where a slow answer feels safe, so if cold calling feels threatening in your class, the climate work has to come first.
pages.wider: Rowe's wait time studies are where this all began, and her line that slowing down may be a way of speeding up is still the best one-sentence case for it.

why: Rowe identified a second wait time that gets far less attention than the first, which is the pause after a student responds. Held for three seconds, it prompts the elaboration and self-correction that an immediate teacher response cuts off.
Silence after an answer signals that more is expected, but if you respond straight away, even warmly, the thinking tends to stop right there.
example: A pupil explains why the graph flattens, and then stops. The teacher says nothing and holds the silence for three seconds, and the pupil adds the condition they'd missed, without being prompted, and corrects their own units along the way.
pages.try: Run both wait times together for a lesson, so three seconds after you ask and three seconds after they answer. The second pause is the harder habit to build, because an answer feels like your cue to speak.
notice: The self-corrections you didn't have to make for them.
Whether answers keep growing past their first full stop.
Whether other pupils come in during the pause without being asked to.
consider: After a wrong answer, the same pause has to read as interest rather than disapproval, and whether it will, in this class, on this day, is your call to make.
Breaking the ask, answer, judge pattern is the bigger project this pause belongs to.
pages.wider: This is the neglected half of Rowe's wait time research, the same three seconds moved to after the answer, where she found it prompts elaboration and self-correction.

why: In open discussion the quickest thinkers set the terms before anyone else has finished forming a view, so a short burst of silent writing before any voice is heard gives every pupil a position of their own to speak from.

The card's phrase makes the argument for it: the pen democratises the room before the voice takes over. On top of this, it leaves you with thirty written answers to glance at instead of three spoken ones to remember.
example: Before a discussion on whether the experiment's results support the hypothesis, the class gets ninety seconds of silent writing. The teacher then opens the discussion by asking a mid-attaining pupil to read out what they wrote, rather than improvising something new on the spot.
pages.try: Try one discussion question tomorrow with ninety seconds of writing first, and take the first contribution from the page rather than from the hand.
notice: Who contributes after writing who wouldn't have contributed before.
The difference in quality between answers read from the page and answers improvised on the spot.
consider: Keep the writing short and rough, because the moment it becomes a task to complete it stops being thinking time and starts being work to mark.
It pairs really naturally with think, pair, share, so pupils write alone, test it on a partner, and then speak.
pages.wider: This belongs to the same body of work as think, pair, share, which is all about structures that give thinking a protected space before it goes public, so discussion can draw on the whole room.

why: Whole-class questioning exposes first-draft thinking to public judgement, which is one reason so many students simply decline to offer any. Lyman's think-pair-share changes the sequence, so there's thinking time alone, then a partner to test the idea on, and only then the room.

By the time an idea is spoken publicly it's already been formed and rehearsed once, and the card's claim is a modest one you can see for yourself: discussion becomes more considered and more substantive.
example: Asked to predict what happens to the current when a second bulb is added, pupils think alone for thirty seconds, then compare predictions with a partner, and then the pairs report back on what they agreed and where they split. The teacher hears reasons, because the pairs have already had to give each other reasons.
pages.try: Take one question you'd normally throw open tomorrow and run it as think, pair, share instead, with the stages timed and kept short.
notice: Contributions from pupils who rarely say anything in open discussion.
Whether the reported answers refer back to the pair talk, along the lines of we thought this, but then.
What actually happens in the think stage, because if pairs start talking straight away, the individual thinking is being skipped.
consider: The think stage is the one that needs protecting, because the value of the structure starts with thinking done alone.
Writing during the think stage makes it visible and harder to skip, and write before you speak is the natural partner here.
pages.wider: Lyman's original structure has barely needed refining over the years, because protected thinking, followed by a low-stakes rehearsal with a partner, followed by the room, still does the job.

why: Hand-raising looks like participation, but Wiliam's point is that it actually distorts it, because a small group volunteers over and over again and the rest learn that waiting patiently works. The pupils you most need to hear from are usually not the ones with their hands up.
Removing hands and directing questions to named pupils changes the contract, because every pupil now owns the possibility of being asked, and that changes how they listen.
example: A teacher tells the class the new normal, which is hands down unless they're asked for, and the teacher will be choosing who answers. Questions go to named pupils across the fortnight, tracked loosely on a class list so nobody stays invisible. The volunteers grumble for a week or so, but the room's attention changes within days.
pages.try: Try it with one class for one week, hands down. Pair it with a visible norm that a wrong attempt is thinking rather than failure, or your quiet pupils will experience it as exposure rather than inclusion.
notice: How the listening changes, because when anyone might be asked, the question belongs to everyone.
Your own selection pattern, because tracking who you ask, even roughly, tends to reveal habits you didn't know you had.
consider: Climate comes first, and the card on cold calling without threat is the necessary companion, because direct questioning is only fair when the room is safe for wrong answers.
Hands still have a place for genuine volunteering, for questions to you, and for contributions you haven't asked for. What changes is who controls how the answering gets shared out.
pages.wider: Good and Brophy's classroom studies documented how questioning patterns can reinforce attainment gaps without anyone noticing, and that's the problem this routine exists to interrupt.

why: Good and Brophy showed that questioning is rarely spread evenly, because teachers direct more questions, and harder ones, to the students they expect more from, and the gap reinforces itself. Cold calling answers that problem, but only if the climate supports it.
Direct questions are only equitable when a wrong answer costs nothing, and the norm the card names carries the whole strategy: no wrong attempts, only thinking.
example: A named pupil offers an answer that's wrong. The teacher treats it as thinking to work with, asks what led them there, and later in the lesson comes back to the same pupil with a related question, so they can see that being wrong didn't take them out of the conversation.
pages.try: Establish the norm before you lean on it. Name it with the class, and hold the room to it the first time a wrong answer draws a reaction.
notice: What actually happens after a wrong answer, both your response and the room's.
The body language of your quieter pupils when names are used, because relief and dread look different.
Whether your harder questions still drift towards the same few students.
consider: Climate is the precondition rather than an optional extra. If cold calling in this class would feel like exposure, the norms come first, and how fast to move with a particular anxious pupil is a call for the teacher who knows the class, not a website.
Hands down is the companion routine, and this card supplies the conditions that make it fair.
pages.wider: Good and Brophy's work on teacher expectations is the evidence base here, and Wiliam's case for questioning every student rests on the same distortion it documents.

why: Almost no teacher believes they distribute questions unevenly until they see their own record. Good and Brophy found harder questions drifting towards higher-attaining students without anyone being aware of it, which is why the remedy is a record, because patterns you can't see in the moment become really obvious on paper.
You can't adjust a habit you can't see, and memory won't give you this picture, but a week of tally marks will.
example: A teacher prints the seating plan and keeps a rough tally for a week, with a mark for each question asked and a second mark when the question was a demanding one. By Friday the plan shows two desks that were never asked anything at all, and the demanding marks clustered on one side of the room.
pages.try: One class, one week, and tally marks on a printed class list or seating plan. Rough is absolutely fine, because rough data you actually collect beats precise data you never do.
notice: Who was never asked anything at all.
Where the harder questions land, and whether the pattern follows attainment, which is what Good and Brophy found.
The gap between what you predicted the tally would show and what it actually shows.
consider: Hands down and cold calling change who you ask, and tracking is how you find out whether they're actually working, so the three cards really make one system.
What to do about a pattern once you can see it is a judgement about individual pupils, and it's yours to make.
pages.wider: Good and Brophy's expectation studies showed differential questioning operating below teachers' awareness, which is exactly why the remedy is a record rather than a good intention.

why: Wiliam's pose, pause, pounce, bounce brings several of this strand's strategies together into one questioning routine. You pose the question to everyone, hold the silence, direct it to a named student, and then bounce the answer to a second student to extend or challenge it.

The bounce is the part that makes this different from ordinary questioning. Because an answer might arrive at anyone, everyone has a reason to listen to it, and the card describes it as keeping all students alert and spreading thinking across the whole room.
example: What was the turning point in this experiment? Then a pause while everyone thinks. Then Jacob is asked, and Jacob answers.
