The teacher doesn't evaluate, but bounces it on instead, asking Priya whether she'd add anything to Jacob's reason or push back on it. The judgement that would normally come from the front comes from the room instead.
pages.try: Script one question through all four steps for tomorrow, including who you might pounce to and who you might bounce to. Improvising the routine can come later, so start deliberate.
notice: The listening during and after the first answer, now that it might land on anyone.
The quality of the bounced response compared with the first answer.
Whether you're pausing for long enough, because without the pause the pounce just becomes a speed test.
consider: Bouncing a wrong answer to another student needs the no-threat climate to be real first, or the first student pays the price for the routine.
The pause is wait time 1 doing its usual work, so the routine inherits everything Rowe found about it.
pages.wider: The routine is Wiliam's, from the same body of formative assessment work as hands down, and Rowe's wait time research explains why the pause isn't optional.

why: Alexander names five qualities of dialogic talk, which are collective, reciprocal, supportive, cumulative and purposeful. The list works really well as a diagnostic, because most classroom talk already meets two or three of the five.

That's what makes this card practical rather than aspirational. You're not building dialogic talk from nothing, you're finding the missing qualities and working on those, so audit first and start with the gaps.
example: A teacher asks a colleague to observe a discussion lesson with just the five words on a slip of paper. The verdict comes back that the talk was clearly collective and supportive, sometimes reciprocal, but rarely cumulative, because contributions sat side by side without building on each other. That one word, cumulative, becomes the focus for the term.
pages.try: Audit one discussion this week against the five qualities, and be honest with yourself. Two or three ticks is the expected result, not a failure.
notice: Which of the five are reliably there in your classroom talk, and which never appear.
Whether contributions chain together, each building on the last, or simply pile up side by side.
Whether the talk is going somewhere planned, which is what purposeful is asking about.
consider: Start with the gaps rather than everything at once, and the card is explicit on this.

Several other cards in this cluster target one quality each, so ground rules build the collective and supportive, and building on responses builds the cumulative. The audit tells you which one to reach for.
pages.wider: Alexander's dialogic teaching is the broadest framework in this strand, and the five principles are its most practical way in.

why: The IRE pattern of initiation, response and evaluation, or ask, answer and judge, is the default grammar of classroom talk, and Alexander shows that it limits thinking, because every exchange is three moves long and ends with a verdict from the front.
The fix on the card is small enough to try today. Replace the evaluation with a follow-up question, such as what makes you say that, so the exchange stays open and the reasoning has to come out.
example: A pupil answers that the metal expands when heated. Instead of saying good, the teacher asks what makes you say that. The pupil explains, and the explanation shows what they think the particles are doing, which turns out to be exactly the thing worth teaching next.
pages.try: Pick one lesson and replace every evaluative response with either a follow-up question or three seconds of nothing at all.
notice: How often you evaluate. The pattern is nigh on impossible to hear from the inside, which is why the card points at capturing a lesson to listen back to.
How long the exchanges become when the third move is a question rather than a verdict.
Whether pupils start justifying their answers before being asked to.
consider: What makes you say that works on right answers too, because probing only the wrong ones teaches the class to read your follow-ups as a signal.
Wait time 2 breaks the same pattern with silence rather than a question, and some exchanges want one and some want the other.

Capturing a lesson to listen back to means recording people, and that needs consent. Whether and how you record is down to your school or trust policy, so seek that answer before you press record rather than after.
pages.wider: Alexander and Mercer both treat IRE as the pattern to escape from, and most of the dialogic cluster is, one way or another, an alternative third move.

why: Mercer distinguishes three kinds of group talk. Disputational talk is I am right and you are wrong, cumulative talk is agreement piled on agreement with nothing examined, and exploratory talk is ideas being challenged with evidence and built on together. Only the third one improves outcomes.

Exploratory talk is what this strand's thinking describes, which is pupils reasoning together and making their thinking public. It seldom appears on its own, which is why the ground rules card follows this one.
example: A group is deciding where to site a settlement. One pupil proposes the valley floor for the water supply, another challenges that with the flood risk shown on the map, and the proposal gets reworked to the terrace above. That's the shape to listen for, with challenge carrying evidence and then building on it.
pages.try: Listen in on one group task this week and ask yourself which of the three kinds of talk you're hearing, because just being able to name which one it is tells you a lot about what to do next.
notice: Whether disagreement comes with evidence or just with volume.
Whether any idea actually changes during the talk, because in cumulative talk nothing does.
Who inside a group is doing the reasoning, and who is just going along with it.
consider: Disputational and cumulative talk aren't misbehaviour, they're what groups default to before the norms of exploratory talk have been taught, and the ground rules card is the companion piece.
tech: A collaborative document or discussion tool from your school's approved set can hold a group's reasoning as it develops and keep it afterwards, so a really useful discussion doesn't disappear the moment the lesson moves on. The test stays the same though, which is that the tool should widen who contributes to the reasoning and never do the reasoning for them.
pages.wider: Mercer's studies of group talk are the source here, and they connect directly to his work on interthinking, because exploratory talk is how thinking becomes genuinely shared.

why: Groups don't fall into exploratory talk by accident. Mercer found that teaching its norms transforms discussion, and there's one detail that changes how you should go about it, which is that norms co-constructed with the class outperform norms that are just displayed or modelled.
The making of the rules is part of the mechanism, because rules a class wrote together are rules they can hold each other to.
example: A class spends ten minutes drafting its own rules for discussion, such as everyone's ideas get considered, reasons are asked for, and we try to agree before we move on. The wording is the pupils' own. It goes on the wall afterwards because they wrote it, not so that they'll read it.
pages.try: Before the next discussion-heavy topic, give ten minutes to agreeing the ground rules with the class instead of presenting yours to them.
notice: Whether pupils bring up the rules unprompted during group work.
Who enforces them when they get broken, you or the group.
consider: It really does need to be co-constructed. The card is explicit that displayed or modelled norms underperform, so it's worth resisting the efficient shortcut even when time is tight.
Success criteria built with the class work by a similar mechanism, which is why the formative assessment strand has a sibling card.
pages.wider: This comes from the same programme of Mercer's research as exploratory talk, and the ground rules are how that kind of talk gets taught rather than just hoped for.

why: Michaels, O'Connor and Resnick's accountable talk holds discussion to two standards at once, which are accurate knowledge and rigorous reasoning. The way in is language, so you teach the moves explicitly, such as I agree because, the evidence is, and say more.
The card's last three words carry the theory: language shapes thinking. If you give pupils the sentence shapes of reasoning, you give the reasoning somewhere to go.
example: During a discussion of a historical source, the sentence starters sit on the board. A pupil begins with the evidence is, and then has to find some in the source before the sentence can end. The stem isn't decorating the claim, it's obliging the pupil to complete it.
pages.try: Introduce two of the moves rather than the whole set, and ask for them in one discussion this week.
notice: Whether the stems are changing the reasoning or just the phrasing around it.
Which moves pupils adopt without being prompted, and whether say more starts passing between pupils rather than only coming from you.
consider: Accountability here is to knowledge and reasoning rather than to talking more, so a short contribution with evidence beats a long one without.
The stems are scaffolds, and scaffolds are there to be faded once the habits of reasoning can stand on their own.
pages.wider: Accountable talk comes from Michaels, O'Connor and Resnick's long programme of work on academically productive talk, and it shares its ground with Mercer, because the quality of talk is teachable.

why: When Alexander's dialogic teaching approach was trialled with the EEF, one teacher move stood out, which was extending student responses rather than evaluating them. The card's image is exactly right: conductor, not judge.

Returning an answer to the room, so Aisha says X, does anyone want to add or challenge, does two things at once. It relieves you of the verdict, and it makes the class the audience for each other's thinking rather than spectators to yours.
example: Discussing a poem's ending, a pupil says it feels hopeful. The teacher returns it to the room, saying Sam thinks the ending is hopeful, and asking who wants to add to that or push against it. Three more contributions arrive before the teacher speaks again, and the third one disagrees with the first, politely, with a line from the poem to back it up.
pages.try: Choose one returning phrase, such as does anyone want to add or challenge that, and use it in place of your usual evaluation for a single lesson.
notice: How long the chains of pupil contributions run before you come back in.
Whether pupils start addressing each other by name rather than routing everything through you.
What your withheld verdict does to the pupil who answered, because the pause after their answer is wait time 2 in action.
consider: Conducting is still steering. You choose whose answer gets returned and when to close a line down, so extending isn't the same as stepping back completely.
Returning a wrong answer for the class to work on needs the same climate as cold calling, or the pupil hears it as being marked in public.
pages.wider: Alexander's EEF-trialled dialogic teaching programme is the direct source, and extending rather than evaluating was one of its core teacher moves.

why: King's finding turns the usual direction of classroom questioning around, because students trained to generate questions from stems produce richer discussion than students who only answer the teacher's questions. Generating a question demands deeper processing than answering one does.
The stems do the heavy lifting here. Without them, student questions tend towards what is X, but with them, pupils reach for connections and consequences they wouldn't have phrased on their own.
example: At the end of an explanation in science, three stems go up on the board, how does ... affect ...?, what would happen if ...?, and how does ... connect to what we learned about ...? Every pupil writes one question about the topic, and a handful get posed back to the class.
pages.try: Put two or three stems up after your next explanation and ask every pupil to write one question before any discussion starts.
notice: The level of the questions against what the stems demand, so are pupils really using the stems, or writing what is X underneath them?
Questions that reveal gaps or misconceptions, because a generated question is evidence as well as enquiry.
How discussion of a pupil's question differs from discussion of one of yours.
consider: Stems need modelling like anything else, so write a few questions with the class before expecting them to manage alone.
The generating is where the processing happens, so the questions are worth something even when there's no time to answer them all.
pages.wider: King's guided questioning studies sit behind this whole cluster, and the stems are her mechanism for lifting student questions above recall.

why: King's reciprocal questioning takes question stems one step further, so students generate questions and pose them to each other, with neither the asker nor the answerer knowing the answer in advance. That last condition is the really interesting one, because it produces genuine enquiry rather than rehearsal.
The card's closing instruction captures the spirit of the whole thing: aim to think.
example: After a fortnight's work on the circulatory system, pairs each write a question using the stems, swap them over, and work on the answers together. One pair lands on a question about why valves fail that neither of them can answer, so they bring it to the teacher, and the question becomes the opening of the next lesson.
pages.try: Run it first on content you've already taught, with the stems provided and ten minutes protected for it, so one question each, then swap, then talk through the answers together.
notice: Whether pairs are enquiring or rehearsing, because questions they already know the answers to are practice rather than this.
The talk while they're answering, which at its best sounds like exploratory talk in miniature.
The questions neither pupil can answer, which are really useful information for you.
consider: Teaching the stems comes first, so this card assumes the previous one.
When a pair is stuck, the temptation to hand over the answer is strong, but a good question is meant to be wrestled with, so give the struggle a little room before you shorten it.
pages.wider: King tested reciprocal peer questioning directly against discussion of teacher questions, and the distinction between enquiry and rehearsal is hers.

why: A student's question reveals the depth of their understanding, and often more precisely than their answer to yours does. Why does X cause Y comes from a different place than what is X, and that difference is diagnostic, so a question works as a window into where a learner actually is.
The routine on the card is deliberately small, which is just one written question from each student before they leave.
example: At the end of a lesson on photosynthesis, every pupil writes one question. They range from what is chlorophyll again to why do plants need glucose if they are making oxygen, and read together, the pile shows you where the class is, so who is still at naming, who is connecting ideas, and which misconception has survived the lesson.
notice: The level of the questions, what against why, and how it shifts across a topic.
Pupils whose questions sit a long way above or below what their written work suggested.
Which questions repeat across the class, because a question lots of pupils ask is a teaching point rather than a coincidence.
consider: The questions are only evidence if they change something, so reading them into the next lesson's plan is the other half of the routine.
Question stems raise the quality of what pupils are able to ask, so the two cards work together.
tech: An approved exit ticket or response tool will gather a question from every pupil in the closing minutes, including the ones who would never ask one out loud, and it keeps the whole set in one place to read while you're planning what comes next. The tool manages the collecting, but the reading, and deciding what to do about it, stays with you.
pages.wider: King's research explains why generating a question is so revealing, and Wiliam's explains what to do with the evidence once you have it.

why: Interthinking is Mercer's word for something classrooms can be unusually good at, which is cognition genuinely shared, built between people through language. Student questions are what keep that joint enquiry moving along.
The distinction the card draws is the one to hold onto here: the goal is thinking in common, not performance for the teacher.
example: A group is working out why their bridge design failed under load, and the questions that move the work along pass between the pupils, such as was it the joints or the span, and how do we test that without breaking the second one. Nothing routes through the teacher, and the enquiry belongs to the group.
pages.try: Sit yourself near one group during a task and count how many of the questions being asked are pupil-to-pupil rather than pupil-to-you.
notice: Whether the questions route through you or pass across the group.
Whether a pupil's question ever changes the group's direction, because that's joint enquiry doing its work.
How the talk changes when you come near, because a group performing for the teacher sounds different from a group that's thinking.
consider: Exploratory talk is the ground this grows in, so groups that haven't learned its norms will find it hard to interthink, whatever the task is.
pages.wider: Interthinking is where Mercer's work on classroom talk ends up, with language not just expressing thought but doing the thinking, jointly.

why: The know and want-to-know routine is familiar enough to feel like habit, but King's research gives it a firmer footing, because questions connected to prior knowledge produce the most powerful learning, and asking students to write what they know and what they want to know surfaces both halves at once.
Their questions become the way into the content, rather than an opening activity that gets filed away and forgotten.
example: Opening a unit on space, pupils write two short lists, what they already know and what they want to know. The teacher reads both before planning the next lesson. The first list shows the prior knowledge to connect to, along with one misconception to unpick, and the second supplies three questions that are good enough to teach through.
pages.try: Give ten minutes at the start of your next new topic to know and want to know, written down and collected in rather than just discussed.
notice: Prior knowledge you didn't expect, in both directions.
Which pupil questions could anchor a whole lesson, and which ones reveal what the class thinks the topic is about.
Whether pupils spot their own questions being answered as the unit unfolds.
consider: It's an entry point rather than an itinerary. The scheme of work still sets the destination, and what to do with the questions it can't accommodate is your call.
Collecting the lists in writing keeps every pupil's starting point visible, and not just the confident talkers'.
pages.wider: King's finding about prior knowledge connects this card to a principle that runs right through the whole guide, which is that new learning holds best when it's fastened to what's already there.

why: New material has a habit of arriving faster than pupils can process it, and Rosenshine's first principle is really clear about the remedy, which is to present new material in small steps with practice after each one, because working memory is narrow and it's easily overwhelmed.
The important thing is the practice after each step, because a step without a check is really just a pause, and telling a class something isn't the same as explaining it to them.
example: Introducing balancing equations, a science teacher builds the method up one move per slide, using animation to reveal each step as it's needed. After each reveal, pupils have a go at one line of a parallel problem on mini whiteboards before the next step comes up.
pages.try: Take one explanation you've already got planned and mark where each genuinely new idea begins. Those marks are your steps, so add a short bit of practice after each one.
notice: Where things start to go wrong. With small steps, confusion shows up at a specific step rather than at the end of a long explanation, which makes it much easier to deal with.
Whether the practice after each step is being done by everyone, or just by the pupils who were already keeping up.
consider: Step size is a judgement about this class and what they already know, and what's one step for a second teaching might be three steps for a first. You know the class, and a website doesn't.
Small steps aren't the same as slow teaching, because checking as you go can save you a much longer reteach later on.
pages.wider: Rosenshine's principles of instruction pulled together decades of research on effective teaching into this sequence, and Sweller's cognitive load theory helps to explain why it works.

why: Abstract ideas are really hard to hold on to when there's nothing to attach them to, and Willingham's advice is to anchor new ideas to concrete examples first, so you make the thing visible and then you name it.
When you name the idea first, the load goes the wrong way round, because pupils are being asked to hold a definition in mind while they're still hunting around for what it actually refers to.
example: Before the word erosion appears anywhere, a geography teacher plays a short clip of a riverbank collapsing, and then shows photographs of the same stretch of river a year apart. Only once the class has described what they can see does the term arrive to label it.
pages.try: For one abstract term you'll be teaching next week, find the image, clip or object first, and plan to show it before you ever say the word.
notice: Whether pupils reach for the concrete example when they're explaining the idea back to you.
What happens when the abstract term is tested later on, and whether the anchor comes back with it.
consider: The concrete example is there to get pupils to the abstract idea, not to stay forever. The card is explicit that you move to the abstract once the concrete is secure, and judging when it's secure is a call only the teacher in the room can make.
pages.wider: Willingham's cognitive science writing for teachers is the source here, and his point is that understanding is built out of things we already understand, which is why the concrete example comes first.

why: Nothing you explain lands on a blank slate, and Rosenshine's advice is to connect to prior knowledge before you introduce anything new, because the new idea has to attach to something that's already there.
Link before you launch, as the card puts it. The few minutes you spend activating what pupils already know might well decide how much of the explanation actually sticks.
example: Before starting a unit on the causes of the First World War, a history teacher puts a concept map on the screen and asks the class to retrieve what they can remember about empire and alliances from the previous term. The gaps that show up then shape how the new explanation begins.
pages.try: Open your next new topic with a two-minute retrieval starter on the specific ideas the explanation depends on, rather than general revision.
notice: What the starter shows you. If the prior knowledge isn't there, the explanation you'd planned needs adjusting before it starts.
Whether pupils use the retrieved ideas of their own accord when they meet the new material.
consider: The starter is there to tell you something, not to decorate the lesson, so be ready to act on what it shows, even if that means reteaching before you launch into the new content.
Choose retrieval targets that genuinely underpin the new content, because activating unrelated knowledge just fills working memory without helping the explanation along.
pages.wider: This is one of Rosenshine's principles of instruction, and it's part of the same distilled research base that gives the strand its small-steps sequence.

why: There's a common assumption that the more sophisticated tool teaches better, but the EEF found otherwise. Clarity matters more than the delivery method, and a simple diagram under a visualiser can outperform a polished video.
So when it comes to any display, the question to ask is not so much whether it's impressive, but whether it makes this idea clearest for this class.
example: Planning to teach the structure of the heart, a science teacher weighs up a slick animation against drawing and labelling the diagram live under a visualiser, and chooses the live drawing, because the class gets to see the structure assembled one part at a time, at the pace of the explanation.
notice: Whether pupils can put the idea back into their own words afterwards, whichever display you went with.
Whether the time spent producing a resource shows up in what the class understood, because effort and clarity aren't the same thing.
consider: Clearest is a judgement about a particular idea and a particular class, and it's a judgement only the teacher in the room can make.
There's nothing wrong with a new tool as such, and the test is simply whether it makes the idea clearer than what you already do.
pages.wider: The EEF's review of digital technology in classrooms sits behind this card, and its finding that clarity beats delivery method is really the whole strategy.

why: A class that's listening politely looks exactly the same as a class that understands, but listening isn't learning, and an explanation that's never checked is really just a guess about thirty minds.
Rosenshine's answer is to check understanding at every step and to reteach before moving on, so the explanation is the start of the process rather than the finish.
example: Halfway through explaining photosynthesis, a teacher poses one question to the whole class and every pupil answers on a mini whiteboard. The spread of answers decides what happens next, so the class either moves on or the step that wobbled gets retaught.
pages.try: Plan one check into the middle of your next explanation, and have everyone answer it at once rather than one volunteer.
notice: The gap between who looked like they were following and who actually showed you they were.
What the wrong answers have in common, because a shared error usually points at the explanation rather than the pupils.
How often the check changes what you do next. If it never does, it's become a ritual rather than a check.
consider: Checking every step changes your pacing, and that's the point rather than a cost, because Rosenshine's sequence assumes you'll sometimes need to reteach.
Whole-class response works better than sampling one or two hands, because the pupils you don't hear from are the ones assumptions tend to get made about.
pages.wider: Checks for understanding sit at the centre of Rosenshine's principles of instruction, and this card is that principle applied to the middle of an explanation rather than the end.

why: Once an explanation is recorded, it's tempting to let the recording do the teaching, but the EEF's finding pushes the other way. Technology works best when it supplements teaching rather than replacing it.
A screencast can't see puzzled faces, take a question or reteach a step, so it works alongside your classroom explanation rather than instead of it.
example: After teaching a method live, a maths teacher posts a short screencast of the same method to the class page. Pupils who were absent, or who just want to see it again before the homework, can replay it, and the live lesson stays exactly as it was.
pages.try: Before you record anything, try to name what the recording adds that the live explanation can't, such as the chance to replay it, pause it or catch up after an absence. If you can't name one, skip the recording.
notice: Who uses the replays, and when, because use that clusters before homework or an assessment tells you something quite different from no use at all.
Whether the questions pupils ask in lessons change once the replays exist.
consider: The live explanation stays primary, and if the screencast starts standing in for your teaching rather than backing it up, the balance has tipped.
tech: A screencast made with the approved screen recording tool in your setting, shared through your school's learning platform, gives an explanation a second life, because pupils can pause it, rewind it and come back to it whenever they need to. That's the supplement. The moment it becomes the first and only telling, it's a substitute, and that isn't where the EEF's evidence says technology works best.
pages.wider: The EEF's digital technology guidance is the direct source, and supplement, never substitute is its finding compressed into four words.

why: Working memory holds around four items at a time, and every element on your screen is bidding for one of those slots. A logo, a border or a sentence nobody needs right now is taking up space the explanation really requires.

Sweller's point is about how the mind works rather than how slides look. Stripping slides back to the essentials is load management, and so is pressing B to blank the screen when you want the attention on you.
example: A teacher preparing to explain supply and demand cuts the slide down to one graph and a four-word heading. When the discussion moves beyond the graph, the B key blanks the screen and the class's four slots can go to the voice doing the explaining.
pages.try: Count the elements on each slide of the deck you'll teach next. Anything beyond the essentials is a candidate for deletion, and the B key covers the moments when the essential thing is you.
notice: Where pupils look during the explanation, both with a full screen and with a blank one.
Whether recall improves on the ideas you taught from stripped-back slides. If nothing changes, have a look at what else is loading the moment.
consider: What counts as essential depends on the idea and the class, so the four-item limit is general but the editing is local.
A blank screen shifts the whole load onto your spoken explanation, which is why this pairs so well with small steps.
pages.wider: Sweller's cognitive load theory supplies the mechanism here. Working memory is narrow and easily overwhelmed, and explaining is really an act of load management.

why: Put the labels in one place and the diagram in another and pupils have to search between them, holding fragments in mind while their eyes travel. Sweller calls this split attention, and all that searching spends exactly the working memory the explanation needs.
Integrating the labels directly into the image takes the searching away. Nothing about the content changes, but reading it costs a lot less.
example: Teaching the water cycle, a teacher shows the diagram unlabelled and then adds each label live with an annotation tool, placing the word on the part it names while that stage is being explained. The class never has to go matching a numbered key to the picture.
pages.try: Find one resource you use where the key or the captions sit apart from the image, and move the words onto the image itself.
notice: Whether the which-bit-is-that questions start to disappear.
How pupils label their own diagrams afterwards, and whether they copy the integrated layout for themselves.
consider: Building the labels live does two jobs at once, because it integrates the information and it paces the reveal to your explanation.
When you can't edit a printed resource, annotating it under a visualiser gets you the same integration.
pages.wider: Split attention comes from Sweller's cognitive load research, and Mayer's spatial contiguity principle is the same insight arrived at through multimedia learning.

why: Reading text aloud while the same text sits on the screen feels thorough, but Sweller's redundancy effect says it's the opposite. Pupils end up processing the written and spoken versions at once, the two streams compete with each other, and working memory pays for both.
The fix costs nothing at all. Say it, or show it, and stop doing both at the same time. Explaining is an act of load management, and this is just about the easiest load there is to remove.
example: Mid-explanation, a teacher presses B, the screen goes black, thirty pairs of eyes come up, and the idea gets explained in speech with nothing competing for attention. When the diagram is needed the screen comes back, and the teacher talks over the image rather than reading beside it.
pages.try: Take one slide you'll teach this week, delete the sentences and keep the image, and say the deleted words instead. The B key, or W for a white screen, does the same job mid-flow.
notice: Where pupils look when the screen is blank, compared with when it's full of text.
What your checks for understanding tell you afterwards. A cleaner explanation should show up as cleaner recall, and if it doesn't, that's worth knowing too.
consider: The effect is about doing both at the same time. Text pupils need to read silently, in their own time, is a different situation and a perfectly legitimate one.
A blank screen puts all the weight on your spoken explanation, which is exactly why this pairs so well with small steps and the other load principles in the strand.
pages.wider: Sweller's cognitive load theory explains the mechanism, and Mayer's multimedia principles map out when words and images combine well and when they collide, and the strand's further reading covers both.

why: Busy slides feel rich but they don't teach much. Mayer's coherence principle is really firm on this, so remove every word, image and sound that doesn't support the learning, because each one competes for attention just when the explanation needs the space.
Clip art, background music and a themed border aren't neutral. If it's on the screen, it's being processed.
example: Rebuilding a slide sequence on the digestive system, a teacher deletes the cartoon stomach, the sound effects and two of the three photographs, leaving one clear diagram and a handful of words. The content being taught is exactly the same, but the competition for attention isn't.
pages.try: Open tomorrow's deck and remove everything decorative from a single slide. Teach it, and see whether anything is actually missed.
notice: Where attention settles once the decoration has gone.
Whether recall centres on the idea itself or on whatever came along with it.
consider: The cuts that feel hardest to make tend to tell you the most. The test isn't whether an element is engaging but whether it supports the learning, and that's where the coherence principle draws the line.
Decoration for one class might be scaffold for another, so what supports learning is judged in the room rather than in the template.
pages.wider: Mayer's coherence principle, part of his cognitive theory of multimedia learning, is the source here, and Sweller's load theory explains what all the clutter costs.

why: Show a class a dense diagram or a long passage and every pupil has to work out for themselves where to look. Mayer's signalling principle offers the fix, because bold, arrows and highlights direct attention to the part the explanation is about.
Without a signal, learners are left searching on their own, and some of them will still be searching when the explanation moves on.
example: Analysing a poem on screen, an English teacher highlights the two words under discussion as they're being discussed, live, with an annotation tool. The whole class is reading the same poem, but everyone is looking at the same two words at the same moment.
pages.try: Next time a text or diagram is on the screen, annotate it live during the explanation instead of presenting it pre-marked.
notice: How quickly eyes find the feature you're talking about.
Whether pupils' own notes and annotations pick out the features you signalled, or whether they pick out different ones.
consider: Signal sparingly, because a slide where everything is bold has no signal at all.
Live annotation ties the signal to your voice, so attention and narration can move along together.
pages.wider: Signalling is one of Mayer's multimedia principles, and it was developed from the same research programme as coherence and segmenting.

why: Delivered as one continuous stream, an explanation gives working memory nowhere to catch up. Mayer's segmenting principle breaks the content into chunks, with processing time in between them.
On screen, that means one idea per click, and the pause after each chunk is where the processing actually happens.
example: A teacher explaining the stages of mitosis sets the diagram to build across five clicks. Between clicks, a question or a ten-second look at the board gives each chunk time to settle before the next one arrives.
pages.try: Take one slide that currently shows everything at once and rebuild it so that each idea appears on its own click.
notice: Whether the pauses that feel long to you actually land differently with the class.
The questions that come up between chunks, which can surface confusion while the idea is still small.
consider: Click, not auto-play. The card is specific about this because the difference is about who controls the pace, and that's you reading the room rather than the software reading a timer.
pages.wider: Mayer's segmenting principle is the direct source, and it's the multimedia expression of the same limit that Sweller's load theory describes.

why: Words and images reach the mind through separate channels, and Paivio's dual coding theory says that using both gives the same idea two routes in.
So when it comes to your slides, pair a key visual with minimal text, and make sure both of them are carrying the one idea.
example: For a lesson on trench warfare, the slide holds one cross-section image and just six words of labelling. The teacher's narration does the explaining, and the image and the sparse text give the idea its second route in.
pages.try: Choose one text-only slide and find the visual that shows its idea, then cut the text down to the few words the visual can't carry.
notice: Whether pupils sketch when they try to recall the idea, and what their sketches keep hold of.
Whether the image comes back when the words are tested later on.
consider: This is two routes to the same idea rather than two ideas at once, so an unrelated image is clutter rather than coding.
Minimal text is part of the theory rather than a style preference, and the redundancy and coherence cards explain what fuller text costs.
pages.wider: Paivio laid out dual coding theory, and Mayer built on it in the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, and this card is really that theory applied to a single slide.

why: An image explained by on-screen text asks the eyes to do two jobs at once. Mayer's modality principle found that people learn better from images with narration than from images with text, because the voice takes one channel and the image takes the other.
Let the voice do what text would overload, as the card has it. The strand prose makes the same call, which is to narrate a diagram rather than captioning it.
example: Recording an explanation of longshore drift, a teacher screencasts the diagram and speaks the explanation over it, with the cursor tracing the movement being described. There are no paragraphs on the screen, so the words arrive by ear while the eyes follow the coast.
pages.try: Take one diagram you usually present with a written explanation beside it, strip the text back to bare labels, and speak the explanation instead, either live or recorded.
notice: Where pupils look while you're narrating, compared with when there was text to read.
On a recorded version, where pupils pause and replay, because those points can map the difficult moments.
consider: Modality moves the explanatory prose to the voice, but short labels that simply name the parts still belong on the image, and that's what the contiguity card covers.
pages.wider: Mayer's modality principle is the source here, and it rests on the dual channel model that Paivio's work established.

why: Every stretch of screen between a label and the thing it names has to be crossed by the eye and bridged by memory. Mayer's spatial contiguity principle keeps words next to the images they describe, so nothing needs holding on to during the journey.
A numbered key below a diagram is the classic offender, because it's accurate and complete and simply in the wrong place.
example: Laying out a slide on the parts of a flower, a teacher places each label beside its structure with a short connecting line, rather than listing the names in a panel down the side, so reading the slide and reading the diagram become the same act.
pages.try: Have a look through the resources for your next topic for separated captions, keys and label lists, and move each word next to the thing it names.
notice: How long it takes pupils to find a named part on the diagram itself.
Whether questions about the diagram use the vocabulary from the labels.
consider: The principle applies wherever words and images share a surface, so worksheets, wall displays and textbook pages as well as slides.
For a resource you can't redesign, annotating it live under a visualiser puts the words where they belong.
pages.wider: Spatial contiguity is one of Mayer's multimedia principles, and it shares its mechanism with Sweller's split attention effect.

why: A finished slide shows everything at once, but an explanation happens over time. Progressive reveal closes that gap by adding content one step at a time, so the display keeps pace with the telling.
Anything that's visible before you reach it risks being read instead of listened to.
example: Building an annotated map of a battle across eight clicks, a teacher adds each movement as it enters the story, so at any moment the screen shows exactly as much as has been explained and no more.
pages.try: Set every element of your next full slide to appear on click, then teach it and only click when the explanation arrives at each element.
notice: Whether the reading ahead stops.
Which reveals you hold back longest when you're teaching live, because those are the steps your explanation needs the most time on.
consider: The reveal serves the narration rather than the spectacle, so a plain appear does the job, and movement for its own sake is really just more clutter.
One idea per click keeps you honest about how much each step is carrying, which is really small steps by another route.
pages.wider: The card draws on both Mayer's segmenting principle and Sweller's account of working memory, because pacing the display is pacing the load.

why: A long recorded explanation is easy to make and hard to use. Mayer's evidence points at images plus voice outperforming text-heavy slides, and the card adds the discipline that goes with it, which is one idea per video, because brevity beats completeness.
Completeness is what the whole library is for, so each clip only has to do one job.
example: A maths teacher records one screencast on expanding a single bracket, with the working shown on screen and the voice narrating over it, and nothing else. The next idea, a second bracket, gets its own separate recording.
pages.try: Record one short screencast this week on the single idea you're asked to repeat most often.
notice: Which clips get replayed, and where pupils pause them along the way.
Whether the repeat explanations that prompted the recording in the first place actually reduce.
consider: One idea per video is the whole discipline, so when a recording starts needing chapters, it's really several videos.
These are supplements to your live explanation rather than a substitute for it, and the strand is firm on that distinction.

How short is short is your call to make, and the reason to keep making it is working memory. It's narrow, and every extra idea in a video competes for the space the first one needs, so when in doubt, split the recording.
tech: The approved screen recording tool in your setting is all this needs, so record the screen, narrate over it and share it through your usual platform. Keep the design rules from the rest of the strand inside the recording too, with minimal text, one clear visual and the voice doing the explaining.
pages.wider: Mayer's multimedia research underpins both halves of the card, both the choice of narrated visuals and the case for keeping each segment small.

why: An explanation delivered in unfamiliar terms is really two lessons squeezed into one, and working memory pays for both at once. Mayer's pre-training principle separates them, so you teach the key terms first and then the ideas.
Learners who already know the words can give the explanation their full attention, and as the card puts it, they can focus on the ideas.
example: Before a lesson on electrical circuits, pupils meet current, voltage and resistance on a vocabulary slide, or in a short pre-lesson video, with a picture for each one. When the main explanation uses the terms, they label something that's already half-known rather than arriving as new noise.
pages.try: List the terms your next explanation can't be given without, and teach the unfamiliar ones before it starts rather than pausing to define them mid-flow.
notice: Whether the questions during the explanation are about the words or about the ideas.
Whether the pre-trained terms start showing up in pupils' own talk and writing.
consider: How many terms need pre-training, and which ones, is a judgement about this class, and you're the one who knows who's meeting each word for the first time.
Pre-training pairs really naturally with connecting to prior knowledge, because one prepares the words and the other prepares the ideas they'll attach to.

stair.lede: Drafting a tight vocabulary list with pupil-friendly definitions is the sort of job AI does really well, through the approved tool in your setting:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary science teacher. From the topic outline below, identify the six terms Year 8 pupils must know before an explanation of the topic, and write a one-sentence pupil-friendly definition for each.

Keep definitions concrete and free of other technical terms. Present as a plain list, term then definition, nothing else.

[paste your topic outline here]
stair.after: You know which terms your class already holds, so cut and swap until the list really is the six that open up the explanation. Iteration is essential, and the definitions need to match how you'll use the terms in the room.

pages.wider: Pre-training is one of Mayer's multimedia principles, and its logic is pure cognitive load theory, which is to reduce what's novel at the moment of explanation.
tech: A vocabulary slide or a short pre-lesson video, made with the approved tools in your setting, puts the terms in front of pupils before the explanation needs them, and that's really all this takes.

why: Experts make invisible decisions all the time, such as where to start, what to check and when something looks wrong. Pupils see the finished product and none of the decisions, and then they're asked to produce the same kind of product themselves.
Thinking aloud while you work makes that invisible expertise visible. It's modelling the process rather than the product, and the process is the thing novices actually need to copy.
example: Under a visualiser, a teacher annotates an unseen source and narrates the decisions as they go: I am reading the provenance line first, because it changes how I weigh everything else. I am not sure about this phrase yet, so I am marking it and moving on. The narration is the lesson, and the finished annotation is really just what's left behind afterwards.
pages.try: Choose one task this week that you'd normally demonstrate silently or show finished, and narrate your way through it live, with the choices, the checks and what you do when you're not sure.
notice: What shows up in pupils' next attempts. Copied structure and copied self-checks are the strategy working, but copied surface features are a sign the narration stayed too shallow.
The questions pupils ask afterwards, which tend to move away from what is the answer and towards how did you know to do that.
consider: Narrating decisions is different from narrating actions. Now I underline the date is just a caption, but I am underlining the date because it tells me which rules apply is thinking made audible.
This is the start of a handover rather than the whole of one, and the strand's scaffolding strategies describe the fade from modelled to guided to independent.
pages.wider: Rosenshine's principles put modelling and worked examples at the centre of effective instruction, and thinking aloud is those principles applied to the parts of expertise pupils can't otherwise see.
tech: The visualiser is the stage here, and a screen recording of the same narration gives pupils the modelling on replay, so they can pause it at the exact moment they lost the thread. Use the approved tools in your setting for both, and remember the technology carries the modelling rather than replacing it.

why: Modelling only teaches the pupils who can actually see it, and a visualiser turns any desk into a stage, so handwriting, annotation and a diagram taking shape are all visible to the whole room at once.

The EEF found the visualiser among the most promising classroom technology, which is quite striking for such a modest device. It doesn't change anything about the work itself, but it makes a huge difference to who gets to watch it happen.
example: Redrafting a paragraph under the camera, an English teacher crosses out, substitutes and rereads in front of the class, with the page filling up with visible second thoughts. The same demonstration at a desk would only have reached the front row.
pages.try: Put one ordinary thing under the visualiser this week, such as your own working, a source or a pupil's draft shared with permission, and teach from it.
notice: Whether every seat genuinely has a sightline, and that includes the corners.
What changes when the work on the stage is a pupil's rather than your own.
consider: The stage is for process. Rosenshine's advice is to model the working rather than display the finished product, and a visualiser makes the crossings-out public, which is really where its value sits.
Sharing pupil work under the camera depends on the culture in the room, and you're the judge of when a class is ready for it.
pages.wider: The EEF's technology guidance supplies the evidence of promise, and Rosenshine's principles supply the reason, because modelling sits at the centre of effective instruction.

why: Sweller and Cooper showed that students can learn more from studying worked examples than from solving equivalent problems, but a worked example on the board only lasts as long as the lesson allows.
Recording it changes things. A screencast of the method can be paused, rewound and studied at each pupil's own pace, which suits the way novices need to see a process unfold.
example: Working a full solution to a quadratic on screen, a teacher records the process, narration included, and posts it to the class page. That evening one pupil pauses at the factorising step three times, and another skims to the final line to check their own working.
pages.try: Record the worked example you were going to do anyway, so just point the approved screen recording tool at it while you teach, and share the result.
notice: Where the pauses and rewinds cluster, if your platform shows you that.
Whether pupils refer back to the method in the middle of their practice, or only check the final answers.
consider: The replay supplements the live modelling, so the thinking aloud, the checks and the questions still happen in the room.
Pairing recorded examples with practice problems, so example then attempt, is where the next card takes this.
tech: A screen recording made with the approved tool in your setting and shared through your learning platform is the whole setup, and the value sits in the replayable method rather than in production polish.
pages.wider: Sweller and Cooper's worked example research is the direct source here, and it's a central finding of cognitive load theory.

why: Teach five examples and then set ten problems and the method has faded before the first attempt. Atkinson's research supports a much tighter weave, which is to alternate worked examples with practice, so an example, then a try, then another example, then another try.
Each attempt comes while the example is still fresh in mind, and each fresh example arrives just after pupils have discovered what they needed it for.
example: On the screen there's a worked percentage-change example, then a structurally identical problem for pupils to try, then a second example with different numbers, then a second attempt. The display alternates between showing and asking for the whole of the practice phase.
notice: Error rates on the first attempt after each example, compared with the long-block approach you might have used before.
Whether pupils look back at the example mid-attempt, and what they look for when they do.
consider: Parallel means genuinely parallel, so the same structure with a different surface. A task that changes the structure is a new example pretending to be practice.
How long to keep alternating before you move to unsupported problems is a fading decision, and that judgement belongs with the teacher who can see the attempts.

stair.lede: The example-try rhythm gets through a lot of parallel practice questions, and drafting them, matched to your worked example, is a really good use of AI through the approved tool in your setting:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary maths teacher. Below is a worked example I will model for Year 9. Create four practice problems that follow exactly the same method and structure, changing only the numbers and surface context.

Order them from most similar to the example to least. Do not include solutions, hints or method notes.

[paste your worked example here]
stair.after: Check that each problem really does exercise the same method, rather than a lookalike that needs a different move, because that's the check only a subject teacher can make. Iterate until the set is right, then run example, try, example, try.

pages.wider: Atkinson's work on alternating examples with practice builds directly on Sweller's worked example effect, and the two are cited together on the card for good reason.
tech: The pattern really doesn't need much, just a display for the example and a task alongside it, using the approved tools in your setting.

why: Support that never fades teaches pupils to depend on the support, but support removed all at once tips them into overload. Rosenshine's resolution is a gradient, so a complete example first, then a partial one with gaps, then independent practice.
The fading is where the teaching happens, because each piece you remove hands one more part of the thinking over to the pupil, at a rate working memory can absorb.
example: A fillable template structures a science evaluation three times over, first fully modelled, then with the reasoning sentences gapped, then blank. The same document, with more taken out each time, walks the class from watching to doing.
pages.try: Take one task you currently model in full and build the middle version, which is the same example with strategic gaps for pupils to complete.
notice: Which gaps get filled confidently and which ones stall a row of pens, because the stalls show you where the thinking actually lives.
Who still reaches for the complete version, and how long they carry on doing so.
consider: The rate of fading is the judgement, and it's made per class and sometimes per pupil. The strand prose says scaffolds are removed as competence grows, and competence is something you judge in the room.
Fading the visible scaffold pairs with fading your own live support, so the template is one strand of a wider handover.
pages.wider: Rosenshine's principles put scaffolding and its removal at the heart of instruction, and Sweller's load theory explains why that removal has to be gradual.

why: Some things just won't come into the classroom, because they're too fast, too slow, too dangerous or too large. The EEF found that simulations let students manipulate variables and see the consequences beyond those physical limits.
The card's caveat is really the heart of the strategy, so use a simulation to extend your explanation, not to replace it. Technology serves pedagogy here, as it does everywhere in the strand.
example: After teaching resistance directly, a physics class opens a circuit simulation and changes one variable at a time, watching the current respond in ways the bench equipment can't safely or visibly show. The explanation came first, and the simulation stretches it.
pages.try: Identify one topic where the real phenomenon can't come into your room, and check whether the approved tools in your setting include a simulation that could extend your explanation of it.
notice: Whether pupils connect what the simulation shows to the explanation that came before it, or treat it as a separate game.
The language pupils use afterwards, because talk of variables and consequences suggests the manipulation did some work.
consider: A simulation with no explanation around it is a substitution, and that's the pattern the EEF's evidence warns against.
Which variables pupils should manipulate, and in what order, is a teaching decision the simulation won't make for you.
tech: Simulation tools and interactive models sit further up the complexity scale than most of the technology in this strand, which makes the strand's rule more important rather than less, so pedagogy informs the approach and the tool enhances and supports. Use the simulation your setting has approved, and use it after the explanation has done its work.
pages.wider: The finding on simulations comes from the EEF's digital technology guidance, which is the same review behind the strand's supplement-never-substitute rule.

why: A vague aim doesn't really give a pupil anything to steer by. "Do your best on question three" isn't something they can check themselves against, and that's why Zimmerman puts a specific, proximal goal right at the start of the self-regulation cycle, so that learners look ahead before they act.

When you ask pupils to say what a good answer to this question would look like, before they start writing it, the aim becomes something they can check their work against while the work is still happening, and that's a really useful thing for them to have.
example: Before a history essay, pupils jot down three things a strong answer to this exact question would need to include. The class compares suggestions and agrees a shared version, and it stays up on the screen while they write. This means a pupil who pauses mid-paragraph now has something concrete to check themselves against.
pages.try: Before your next extended answer, try asking "what would a good answer to this include?" and take suggestions before anyone writes a word. It takes two minutes and there's no preparation needed.
notice: Whether the goals pupils come up with are specific, or just the task said back to you. "Write a good essay" is really just the vague aim in a slightly different form.
Whether anyone refers back to the goal while they're working. A goal that gets set and then ignored isn't really part of the cycle yet.
Whether the goal they've stated actually changes what gets written.
consider: Pupils who are new to this will come up with woolly criteria at first, and that's a reason to model the move for them rather than a reason to give up on it.
The long-term aim is pupils who set the goal without being asked. The prompt is a scaffold, and like any scaffold it's there to be faded over time.
pages.wider: Goal-setting sits in the forethought phase of Zimmerman's self-regulation cycle, and it's the looking ahead that makes the later monitoring and self-judgement possible.

why: There's a tempting version of metacognition where pupils are taught to plan, monitor and reflect as a free-standing skill. Willingham's point cuts right through it, because you simply can't plan or monitor a task you know nothing about, and a pupil can't judge whether their circuit explanation is going wrong if they don't know the circuit rules.
So the order really does matter here. Teach the content first, because metacognition works on knowledge, never instead of it.
example: Before a science extended task that asks pupils to plan and self-check their approach, the teacher runs a short retrieval starter on the underlying content. Pupils who can't yet retrieve the basics get more practice on those before they're asked to do the planning and monitoring steps, so the regulation is only ever pointed at material that's actually there to be regulated.
pages.try: Put a retrieval starter in front of your next task that asks for planning or self-checking, and let the results tell you who's ready to regulate and who still needs more time with the content.
notice: Pupils whose reflections are vague or generic. Often the gap is in the knowledge rather than in the reflective skill.
Whether the quality of pupils' plans follows how secure their content is. It usually does, and that's really the card's argument in miniature.
consider: This does cut against bolt-on study skills lessons taught separately from subjects. Build the base first, then regulate, and do both inside the topic itself.
pages.wider: Willingham's wider argument is that thinking skills depend on knowledge of the thing being thought about, and the same warning against teaching metacognition in the abstract runs right through the strand's evidence base.

why: The first minute of a task is often spent writing, and that's actually the problem. Zimmerman found that strong learners break a task down into its demands before they start, whereas weaker learners answer the question they assumed they were asked, and they only find out at marking time.
Two questions do most of the work here. What is this question really asking, and which topics that you've already covered does it draw on? Both of these come before the first line goes down.
example: A worded maths problem goes up on the board. Before anyone solves it, the class annotates it together, so the quantity that's actually being asked for gets circled, the topics it draws on get named at the side, and the step most likely to catch people out gets a warning mark. Only then do pupils have a go at it, and the annotation stays up where they can see it.
notice: Pupils who start writing the moment the task lands. Starting quickly isn't really a good sign here.
Whether the demands pupils identify match the ones you had in mind, because the mismatches tell you what to model next.
Misreadings coming to light during the analysis rather than in your marking pile, which is the strategy doing exactly what it's there for.
consider: Model the analysis out loud before you expect pupils to do it, because the questions look obvious to an expert precisely because the expert no longer notices themselves asking them.
It does cost a few minutes at the start of the task, so budget for them, but you'll usually find they get repaid at the end.
pages.wider: Task analysis is the opening move of Zimmerman's forethought phase, and it's the reading of the demands that everything downstream, the goal, the strategy and the monitoring, depends on.

why: Most pupils don't really choose a method at all, they just reach for the first one that comes to mind, or the one they always use. Flavell's point is that planning means selecting an approach rather than defaulting to one, and that selection only happens when there's a moment of deliberate choice.
Asking pupils to name which method they'll use for this problem, and why, before the first line goes down makes that choice visible, both to them and to you.
example: A pair of simultaneous equations goes up, alongside a short menu of the methods the class has been taught, such as substitution, elimination and graphing. Each pupil writes the method they're going to use and one line of reasoning in the margin before they start. The teacher scans the reasons rather than just the choices, because "the coefficients already match" is a really different answer from "it's the one I like".
pages.try: On the next task with more than one sensible route through it, ask for the method and the why in the margin before anyone starts. It only costs thirty seconds.
notice: Pupils who pick the same method every time regardless of the problem, because that's habit rather than planning.
Whether the reasons they give mention features of the task itself. When they do, that's conditional knowledge starting to form.
consider: Pupils can only select from strategies they've actually been taught, so if the menu is empty, teach the methods first and come back to this.
The why counts for more than the choice, and a defensible reason for the "wrong" method is actually better planning than a lucky default.
pages.wider: Flavell's metacognitive knowledge includes knowing your own strategies, and Winne adds the conditional layer on top of this, which is knowing which one this particular task calls for.

why: Confidence that's built on pep talks doesn't tend to survive contact with a hard task. Zimmerman's finding is that self-efficacy drives effort, but it has to be earned through past success rather than simply asserted.

Pointing a pupil back to a recent task they genuinely mastered sets a credible expectation for the one in front of them. It's not "you can do anything", it's "you did something like this three weeks ago, and here it is".
example: Before a demanding analysis essay, pupils reopen a marked piece from earlier in the term where they handled a similar demand well. Each pupil names one thing they did then that applies now, such as a planning move or a way of using evidence, so the expectation for the new task is anchored to something that actually happened.
pages.try: Before the next task your class will find daunting, name one specific success they've already earned and say exactly why it's relevant. It has to be specific and true, or it doesn't work.
notice: Whether reluctant starters begin sooner when the anchor is there in front of them.
Whether pupils can say what made the earlier success happen. "I worked hard" is a start, but a named method is better, and it connects to how they explain their results.
consider: The reference really does have to be genuine, because a hollow example just reads as a pep talk, and the card is explicit that pep talks are not where efficacy comes from.
For a pupil with little recent success in your subject, choosing what to anchor to takes some care, and you know your class far better than any website does.
pages.wider: Self-efficacy belongs to Zimmerman's forethought phase, because the expectation a learner carries into a task shapes the effort and the persistence they bring to it.

why: Feeling that you understand something isn't evidence that you actually do. Winne showed that a novice's sense of understanding is unreliable, and it's least reliable exactly when it feels strongest, which is just after re-reading familiar material.
The fix is structural rather than motivational. Pair every self-check with an external test, such as a quiz or a worked answer, so that the monitoring rests on evidence rather than on confidence.
example: At the end of a topic segment, pupils rate how secure they feel on it, then straight away take a five-question quiz. The two results sit side by side. For some pupils they'll agree, but for others the quiz disagrees with the feeling, and that disagreement is really the most useful thing the lesson produces.
pages.try: Next time you hear yourself ask "are we happy with this?", follow it up with three quick questions and let the answers do the replying.
notice: Pupils who were confident and wrong. They're the reason the external check exists in the first place.
Whether pupils start asking for the check themselves, because that's the habit starting to become their own.
consider: Keep the checks low-stakes. The point is calibration rather than judgement, and stakes tend to distort both.
The check has to lead to something being done, because a gap that gets discovered and then ignored hasn't really helped anyone.
tech: A self-marking quiz in your setting's approved tool gets the evidence back while the feeling of understanding is still fresh, and that's when the comparison teaches most. The important thing is to be clear about the division of labour, because the tool supplies the evidence, but the pupil still does the judging of what it means and what to do next, and that part isn't for automating.
pages.wider: Winne's model of self-regulated learning puts flawed self-monitoring right at its centre, because learners regulate on the basis of what they believe about their progress, so those beliefs need correcting with evidence.

why: Monitoring your own attention is a skill in itself, and Zimmerman's point is that it develops best in a low-distraction environment to begin with. A pupil can't really practise noticing their focus slipping while twelve tabs are competing for it.

So you scaffold the environment to start with, and then withdraw the scaffold as pupils show they can manage their attention themselves. If the restriction never lifts, the tool is doing the regulating, and the capacity never gets built.
example: During on-screen independent work, the teacher uses the school's classroom management tool to limit what can be open for the first few weeks of the routine. As pupils show they can hold their focus, the limits are relaxed, class by class or pupil by pupil, until managing the screen is their job rather than the software's.
pages.try: Before you switch any restriction on, decide what the first step of switching it off will look like, and what evidence would tell you it's time.
notice: What happens when a restriction lifts, because that first unrestricted session tells you whether focus was actually being learned or just enforced.
Pupils who only work while they know the tool is active. That's exactly the dependency the fading is designed to avoid.
consider: Don't skip the fading. A monitoring tool that's used permanently takes away the very work that builds the capacity, and a guide that always hands you the answer just leaves you needing the guide.
When to fade, and for whom, is a judgement call, and you know your class far better than any website does.
tech: The card names a classroom management tool, so use whichever one is approved in your setting, and hold it to the strand's rule, which is to scaffold the regulation and then fade the scaffold. The aim is a learner who no longer needs the tool.
pages.wider: Structuring the environment is one of the self-regulatory strategies Zimmerman documented in the performance phase, and the handover from external structure to self-management is where the learning actually sits.

why: Left alone, monitoring tends to fade. Winne's observation is that pupils who are absorbed in a task stop checking whether the approach is still working, and the longer they go on, the harder a wrong method is to let go of, because all that sunk effort argues for carrying on.
Planned pauses interrupt that drift. A stop point is simply a scheduled moment where the question "is this still working?" gets asked, whether or not anyone felt like asking it.
example: Fifteen minutes into an extended writing task, a timer marks the stop point. Everyone pauses and answers one question, which is whether their approach is still working and how they know. A pupil whose structure has drifted away from the question notices now, with half the time still left, rather than at the end with none of it.
pages.try: Add one timed pause to the longest task you set this week, with the question written on the board so pupils actually meet it rather than skip past it.
notice: Whether anyone actually changes course at a stop point, because pauses that never alter what pupils do aren't really monitoring yet.
Answers that become routine. "Yes, fine" written in four seconds means the check has turned into a ritual, and rituals need refreshing.
consider: Too many stop points just become noise, and they interrupt the very concentration they're meant to protect. One or two per task is plenty, placed where a wrong turn would be costly.
The external prompt carries the remembering-to-check for pupils, so their attention can stay on the work itself, and that's exactly why the prompt can later be faded rather than kept forever.
pages.wider: Winne's contribution to the strand is precisely this, that regulation happens while the work is happening, not just after it's finished, and it needs prompting until it becomes a habit.

why: Pupils usually discover they didn't understand something when the work comes back marked, and that's the most expensive possible moment to find out. Monitoring during the task, asking do I actually understand this, brings the gap to light while there's still time to do something about it.
The question sounds trivial, but the habit isn't, because self-regulation has to be taught, modelled and practised rather than picked up from simply being told to reflect.
example: Before an extended task, a teacher plants two checkpoints in it. At each one, pupils stop and answer in the margin whether they're sure about what they've just done or whether they're guessing. A pupil who writes guessing at checkpoint one has just saved themselves twenty minutes of confidently wrong work.
pages.try: Plant one checkpoint in one task this week, with the question written where pupils will meet it. Asking them to answer it in writing, even with one word, stops the check being skipped.
notice: Pupils who answer yes and are wrong. A novice's sense of understanding is unreliable, which is why this pairs with an external check rather than replacing one.
Whether anyone changes course after a checkpoint, because monitoring that never alters what pupils do isn't really doing its job yet.
consider: There has to be something to monitor. Metacognition works on knowledge, never instead of it, so the content has to be taught before the checking of it can mean anything.
The prompts are scaffolding, and scaffolding is there to be faded, so the long-term aim is pupils who ask the question without needing the checkpoint.
pages.wider: Flavell gave us the language of metacognition, and Winne showed why the monitoring has to happen while the work is happening rather than just after it's finished.

why: Regulation you can't see is really hard to coach. A finished product tells you whether a pupil got there, but it says almost nothing about the route they took, and the route is where the regulation succeeds or falls down.

Flavell's work is the ground here, because pupils can become more aware of their own thinking, and a brief written trace of their reasoning is that awareness made into something you can actually look at, both you and them.
example: Working through a multi-step maths problem, pupils add a one-line note at each step saying why they took it. When the teacher reviews the traces, they find a pupil whose method is sound but aimed at the wrong quantity from step one. The product was wrong, but the trace shows exactly which part of the process wasn't.
pages.try: Ask for a single margin note on the next problem, along the lines of "why I chose this step". One line is plenty to start with.
notice: The mismatches, such as tidy products built on shaky reasoning and rough products built on sound reasoning. Both of these are invisible without the trace.
Traces written after the event to justify the answer. Explaining it afterwards is a really different activity from showing your working.
consider: Keep the trace brief, because if writing about the thinking starts competing with the thinking itself, the scaffold has taken over from the task.
The trace is for looking at and coaching from, not for marking, so say that out loud, or pupils will write it for the grade.
tech: A shared document in your setting's approved platform lets the trace build up where you can see it during the task, rather than after the books close. That's invisible thinking made visible while there's still time to act on it, and the document shows you the process, but the coaching of it stays with you.
pages.wider: Flavell gave us the language for pupils' awareness of their own thinking, and the trace turns that awareness into something a teacher can actually work with.

why: When you ask pupils to check their work, most of them check how it feels, and "it feels done" tends to win. Zimmerman's point is that self-judgement needs a reference rather than a hunch, because evaluating without a standard is really just mood.
Giving pupils the mark scheme or an exemplar to compare against turns "is it good?" into "does it do what this does?", and that's a question they can actually answer.
example: Pupils lay their own paragraph beside an exemplar, with the mark scheme between them, and identify one criterion their work meets and one it misses. The judgement is a comparison with something real, and the missed criterion becomes the obvious next thing to work on.
pages.try: In your next self-assessment moment, swap "check your work" for "compare your work to this", and put the this in front of them.
notice: Whether pupils' judgements of their own work drift closer to yours over time, because calibration against a standard is something they can learn.
Pupils who can recite the criteria but can't find them in their own writing. Reading an exemplar is a skill in itself, and it needs teaching too.
consider: Choose the exemplar to show the standard rather than perfection. Work that's just above the pupil's current level gives the comparison something to hold on to.
This pairs really naturally with goals set before the task, because the standard used at the end means more when it was in view at the start.
pages.wider: Zimmerman's self-reflection phase turns on comparing performance against a standard, and this strategy simply makes sure the standard is real and present rather than imagined.

why: What a pupil says to themselves after a result shapes what they do with the next one. Zimmerman's finding is that attribution feeds forward, so a result explained by fixed ability, "I'm just bad at maths", closes the conversation down, because ability can't be changed by Tuesday.
A result explained by method stays open, though. The method they used can be named, looked at and altered, and that's why you steer the attribution towards it.
example: When an assessment comes back, the reflection prompt asks which part of how you prepared helped most, and what would you change about how you prepare next time. A pupil who writes "self-quizzing worked, I left the second topic too late" has produced something they can actually use. "I'm not a science person" would have produced nothing at all.
pages.try: Change the question you ask after results, starting with your written comments. Method questions model method attributions.
notice: The language pupils reach for unprompted after results. Ability talk and method talk are easy to tell apart once you start listening for them.
