Whether a changed explanation changes the next preparation, because attribution is only doing its work when it feeds forward.
consider: Your own feedback language carries most of the weight here, and praise aimed at the strategy rather than the person is this card at work in your marking.
Method attributions do have to be true. If the preparation was genuinely fine and the paper was just brutal, say so, because honesty is what keeps the reflection worth doing.
pages.wider: In Zimmerman's cycle the self-reflection phase feeds the next forethought phase, and attributions are the hinge between the two, which is why they're worth steering.

why: A great deal of classroom reflection ends at the reflection. "I should be more careful" gets written, the book closes, and nothing is different on Monday. Butler is really clear on this, that feedback only regulates learning if it changes the next action.
So each reflection gets turned into one concrete adjustment, named and attached to the very next task. Reflection only really counts as metacognition when it changes what the learner does next.
example: After a marked assessment, each pupil writes a single line in an action log, such as next time I will plan for five minutes before writing, or next time I will check units before moving on. The log travels forward with them, and it's open on the desk at the start of the next comparable task, so the plan is there when the moment to use it comes round.
pages.try: End your next reflection activity one step later than usual, so not "what went wrong?" but "what will you do differently on the next one, specifically?"
notice: Adjustments that can be checked versus adjustments that are really just wishes. "Try harder" can't be verified, but "plan for five minutes first" can.
Whether the log actually gets looked at when the next task arrives, because an action log nobody reopens isn't helping anyone.
The same adjustment turning up twice, because that repeat is telling you the loop hasn't closed.
consider: One adjustment, not five, because a single specific change can actually be made and actually be checked.
The gap between tasks makes a difference too, because the next comparable task needs to arrive while the plan is still fresh, and sequencing tasks so that it does is your end of the bargain.
pages.wider: Butler's model treats self-regulation and feedback as one loop, and what a learner notices about their own work only helps insofar as it changes the next attempt.

why: Pupils are usually most confident about the material they met most recently, rather than the material they actually know, and that miscalibration drives poor revision decisions all the way to the exam hall.
Prediction makes the calibration visible. Pupils write the score they expect, see the score they got, and the gap between the two becomes evidence they can learn from, week on week.
example: Before handing in a low-stakes quiz, every pupil writes a predicted score in the corner. When the quizzes come back, they log predicted against actual and note which direction they missed in. After four quizzes, one pupil can see that he always overestimates on definitions and underestimates on application, and that changes how he plans his revision.
pages.try: Add the predicted-score corner to your next low-stakes quiz. The comparison takes a minute when the quiz is returned, and the value builds up over repetitions rather than arriving in week one.
notice: The direction of the error, which tells you more than its size. Systematic overconfidence and systematic underconfidence need really different conversations.
Whether the gaps narrow over time, because the card's phrase, monitoring corrected by evidence, is exactly what you're after.
consider: Keep the stakes low, because the moment a prediction affects anything that counts, pupils start managing the prediction instead of learning from it.
This works best attached to a regular quizzing routine you already run, rather than as a reason to invent a new one.
pages.wider: Winne's work on calibration sits behind this, alongside Dunlosky and Metcalfe's finding that confidence tracks recency rather than knowledge, and the strand's further reading takes both of these further.

why: Reflection is usually treated as the pupil's business, so they notice their errors and they act on them. Butler's insight is that self-regulation and instruction are a loop, and the teacher is inside it, which means that what pupils notice about their own errors is evidence you can plan from.
It changes how pupils treat reflection too, because when Monday's lesson visibly begins from what they reported on Friday, reporting honestly starts to have a point.
example: At the end of the lesson, an exit poll asks each pupil to name the error they made most, or the step they felt least sure of. The teacher tallies the responses, and the next lesson opens by reteaching the most common one, saying so out loud, along the lines of most of you said the same thing, so that's where we're starting.
pages.try: Ask one exit question this week, such as "which part are you least sure of?", and then act on the tally where the class can see you doing it.
notice: Whether what pupils report matches the errors actually in their work. When it doesn't, that mismatch is your next teaching point about self-monitoring.
Whether the self-diagnosis gets sharper once pupils see their reports being used. Consequences tend to improve the reporting.
consider: The visible acting-on is what makes this work, because collected reflections that just vanish teach pupils that reflection is paperwork.
Where the reports and the work disagree, the reflection is still useful, just in a different way, because it tells you the monitoring needs teaching, and not only the content.
pages.wider: Butler frames instruction and self-regulation as a single loop rather than as parallel tracks, and this strategy is that loop run deliberately, with your next teaching move as its output.

why: "Go and revise" assumes pupils already own methods to revise with, and many of them simply don't. Flavell's point is that students cannot deploy a strategy they have never been taught, and what fills the gap is usually re-reading and highlighting, because those don't need any instruction.
Retrieval, spacing and self-explanation all have to be taught explicitly, as named methods with steps, before you can reasonably expect pupils to use them independently.
example: A teacher spends part of a lesson teaching self-quizzing as a method in its own right, so pupils learn what it's called, how to build questions from their notes, and how to check their answers honestly. The class practises it together on current content, the steps go onto a reference sheet, and only after guided practice does it start appearing in homework instructions by name.
pages.try: Pick one strategy your instructions currently assume pupils have, and teach it explicitly this half term, with the name, the steps and the practice all included.
notice: Whether pupils use the method's name themselves. Named strategies get chosen, and vague ones tend to dissolve back into re-reading.
What revision actually looks like when you ask pupils to show you rather than tell you. The gap between the methods they claim and the ones they really use is usually quite telling.
consider: Explicit teaching, then guided practice, then independence, in that order, because expecting the third without the first two is exactly where "go and revise" falls down.
Teach the strategy inside the content it serves rather than in the abstract, because a method learned on real material travels much better into use.
pages.wider: Flavell counted knowledge of strategies among the foundations of metacognition, and the EEF's guidance draws the same line, putting explicit strategy instruction before independent use.

why: Owning a strategy isn't the same as knowing when to reach for it. Winne calls this conditional knowledge, and he argues it's what separates skilled learners, so it's not so much a bigger toolbox as a better sense of which tool this particular task calls for.
That means teaching the cues too, the features of a task that signal which method fits, and not just the methods themselves.
example: The teacher shows two worked cases side by side, with a vocabulary-heavy topic matched to flashcards and spaced review, and an essay question matched to planning plus self-explanation. The question to the class isn't "what are these methods?" but "what was it about each task that made that the right match?"
pages.try: Next time you name a strategy in class, add the when as well, which means the one or two task features that make it the right call here.
notice: Pupils' answers to "why this method for this task?". Answers that mention features of the task are conditional knowledge arriving.
Strategies misapplied with full confidence, such as flashcards aimed at essay skills. The method is fine, but the matching is where the gap is.
consider: Conditional knowledge grows from comparing cases, so one example isn't enough, and it's the contrast that makes the cues visible.
If your class keeps a strategy reference sheet, add a when column to it, because the cue belongs right next to the method.
pages.wider: Winne's account of self-regulated learning gives conditional knowledge, knowing which strategy suits which conditions, the deciding role in whether the regulation actually helps.

why: For self-regulation to develop, the support does have to come away at some point, and Zimmerman is really clear on this. If a pupil is always prompted to plan, check and reflect, they never get the opportunity to remember to do it for themselves, and that's the bit we're actually after.

The route runs from modelled to guided to independent use, with prompts removed as pupils show they no longer need them. Self-regulation has to be taught, modelled, practised and gradually handed over, and it's that gradual handing over this card focuses on.
example: Essay planning prompts follow a planned retreat across the year, so there's a full prompt sheet modelled and used in the autumn, a shortened cue card in the spring, and by the summer a blank page, with the cue card still available to the pupils whose work shows they need it.
pages.try: Choose one prompt that's been in place so long it never gets questioned, and decide what evidence would tell you it can start to fade.
notice: What happens on the first unprompted task, because that's the honest measure of whether the scaffold was teaching or just substituting.
Pupils still receiving prompts they clearly no longer need. Fading late has costs too, because support pupils have outgrown just gets in the way of the independence you're after.
consider: Fade by readiness rather than by the calendar, and not necessarily whole-class either. Who's ready is a judgement only the teacher in the room can make.
Fading isn't final either. A pupil who struggles without the prompt gets it back, and the fade simply restarts from there.
pages.wider: Zimmerman traced the development of self-regulation from observing a model through to independent use, and the strand's whole argument about tools and prompts, scaffold then fade, is that trajectory applied.

why: Pupils keep study methods the way anyone keeps habits, because they're familiar and they feel productive, not because they've actually checked. Re-reading survives on exactly this. Winne's finding is that learners refine an approach by checking whether it worked, which means the checking has to be arranged.
So the idea is that pupils trial a method, judge it against their results, and keep only what the evidence supports, so they're testing their own studying in the same way they'd test anything else.
example: For three weeks, pupils log one line before each weekly quiz saying which method they used to prepare. Afterwards they add the score. At the end they read their own log, and one pupil finds that the evenings spent recopying notes went with their lowest scores, and the ten-minute self-quiz with their highest. The log makes the case, so the teacher doesn't have to.
pages.try: Attach a one-line method log to a quiz routine you already run. The routine is already there, so the logging is the only new bit.
notice: Comfort methods that the log shows aren't doing much. Watching a pupil meet that evidence is the strategy doing its work.
Whether anyone actually drops a method. Keeping the winner is easy, but dropping the familiar loser is the hard part, and it's the part worth praising.
consider: This needs a regular assessment rhythm to judge against, because without one there's no evidence for the log to collect.
Single data points mislead, so judge across weeks rather than after one quiz, because one bad Friday doesn't really tell you much about a method.
pages.wider: Winne describes self-regulated learners as running a feedback loop over their own methods, evaluating each one against outcomes and updating as they go, and this strategy builds that loop where pupils can see it.

why: A strategy taught in the abstract tends to stay there. Willingham's argument is that strategies don't float free of subjects, because self-regulating an essay isn't the same act as self-regulating a proof, and pupils taught "metacognition" in general often can't find it again once they're inside geography.
So each strategy gets taught inside the content it serves. Pupils learn to self-regulate this topic, in this subject, and the strategy arrives already attached to somewhere it works.
example: Rather than sending the class off to a generic study skills session, the geography teacher teaches self-quizzing inside the rivers topic, using rivers vocabulary, and adds it to a subject strategy bank, so the class knows which methods suit map skills, which suit case studies and which suit extended writing. The strategy and the content get learned as one thing.
pages.try: Take one strategy that's currently taught generically in your school and re-teach it inside the topic where it pays off most in your subject.
notice: Whether pupils use the strategy in the subject where they learned it but nowhere else. Transfer is genuinely hard, so expect to teach the strategy again in new territory rather than assuming it travels on its own.
Whether the strategy bank actually gets used, or whether it only really exists as a display.
consider: This makes strategy instruction every department's job rather than a discrete course, and a subject-specific bank is only really credible when the subject's own teachers built it.
pages.wider: Willingham has long argued that thinking skills are bound to the content they operate on, and the same warning against content-free metacognition runs through the strand's evidence base.

why: Spacing is usually something that's done to pupils, so the teacher builds the retrieval schedule and the pupils turn up to it. That works, but it leaves the regulation with the teacher. Deciding when you're going to study is a planning act in itself, and it's one that can be handed over.
Teaching pupils to set their own calendar reminders to revisit topics puts the spacing schedule in their hands, and that's the point where a classroom routine starts becoming a study habit.
example: At the end of a topic, pupils set three reminders on their calendar, one a few days out, one a fortnight out and one a month out. Each reminder names an action rather than a topic, such as quiz myself on the glossary or redraw the diagram from memory. When it fires, the review is ten minutes, and it's retrieval rather than re-reading.
pages.try: Do it together in class the first time, and check that the wording of each reminder names something to do rather than something to look at.
notice: Whether reminders name actions or just topics. "Revise photosynthesis" fires and gets dismissed, but "self-quiz on the photosynthesis flashcards" fires and gets done much more often.
Whether pupils set their own reminders for later topics without being told, because unprompted scheduling is the handover actually happening.
What actually happens when a reminder fires. Ask them, because the answer tells you whether the system is real.
consider: The reminder is only the trigger, and the review it triggers has to be retrieval, or the schedule is just spaced re-reading.
Start with a class-set schedule and fade towards pupil-set, just like any other scaffold in this strand.
pages.wider: Zimmerman would file this under forethought, because it's planning applied to study time itself. The evidence on spacing that it draws on sits with the retrieval practice strand.

why: Writing a good question is harder than answering one, and that's exactly where the value is. To build a quiz from your own notes you have to judge which ideas carry the topic, what's likely to be asked, and what a fair test of it would look like, and every one of those is a monitoring decision.
The tool then supports retrieval the pupil has authored themselves, rather than serving up someone else's judgement of what counts.
example: Pupils turn their notes on a topic into ten flashcards. The constraint does the teaching here, because each card front has to be answerable without giving the answer away, which forces decisions about what the essential knowledge actually is. The finished deck then drives their retrieval practice for the weeks that follow.
pages.try: End a topic with "write five questions a classmate should be able to answer", then swap them over and answer. That's authoring and retrieval in one move, and there's no technology needed to start.
notice: Questions that only go after the easiest facts. That's a judgement gap, and it's teachable, so show them what a probing question looks like and let them revise their own.
Whether the quality of the questions improves once pupils have seen some good models.
consider: The authoring is where the thinking happens. A downloaded deck has had all the deciding done already, and the deciding is precisely the part the pupil needed to do.
Swapping questions gets you a second benefit too, because answering a peer's questions is another retrieval pass, from a different angle.
tech: A flashcard or low-stakes quiz tool approved in your setting will happily manage the practice, so it can store the deck, shuffle the order and bring cards back over time. What it mustn't manage is the writing of the questions. Keep the authoring with the pupil and let the tool carry the admin, which is the strand's rule about scaffolds applied to a quiz app.
pages.wider: Winne's account of self-regulated studying underpins this, because deciding what to ask yourself is itself a monitoring judgement, made before a single answer is attempted.

why: The environment a pupil has to regulate now includes the one in their pocket. Managing attention used to mean choosing a seat away from your friends, and it now also means deciding what the device is allowed to do while you work.

The card's distinction is between imposed and chosen. Teaching pupils to switch on focus modes and silence alerts as a deliberate act puts the regulation with them, so the tool ends up serving their attention rather than pulling it away.
example: Independent study begins with a standing routine, so before anything else, pupils set their device to focus mode and silence their notifications, in the same way they get their equipment out. The step takes seconds. Over time the teacher stops cueing it, and watches to see who still does it.
notice: Who reaches for focus mode unprompted once the cueing stops, because that's the habit either forming or not.
What pupils say when you ask them why they do it. A rule being followed and a choice being understood sound really different, and only the second one survives leaving school.
consider: The point is that the pupil makes the choice deliberately. A block imposed from above does the regulating for them, and that has its place as an early scaffold, but this card is about handing that job over to the pupil.
What pupils can control on school-managed devices varies, so build the routine within your setting's device policy and around the settings pupils genuinely own.
pages.wider: Zimmerman documented environmental structuring as a strategy self-regulated learners use deliberately, and the screen is simply the newest environment to structure.

why: Willingham's line, that memory is the residue of thought, is the whole argument here. A pupil who offloads the thinking to AI hasn't done any thinking, so there's no residue, and nothing gets learned, however polished the work looks.

The distinction the card draws is between AI producing the reasoning and AI challenging reasoning the pupil has already done. The first is substitution, and it hollows out the very capacity this strand is trying to build. The second can work like an external check, provided the judging of the critique stays with the pupil.
example: A pupil finishes a written argument, then asks the approved AI tool to find the weakest step in their reasoning. The tool points at a paragraph, and the pupil now has a decision to make, which is whether the critique is right and, if so, what changes. They revise, or they reject the critique with a reason, and either way the reasoning, both rounds of it, was theirs.
pages.try: Trial it on work that's already finished, so the only thing the tool can touch is the checking. The order, thinking first and tool second, is the whole safeguard.
notice: Pupils who accept the critique wholesale. Handing your judgement over to the critic is offloading too, just one step later.
Whether the revisions show the pupil's own reasoning about the critique, or just compliance with it.
What the work looks like when the tool isn't available, because that's your check on whether any of the thinking has actually stuck.
consider: This sits inside your setting's policy on pupil AI use, and where pupils can't use such tools directly, the same critique step works with a peer or a mark scheme instead.
A pupil with nothing on the page yet has nothing for a critic to work on, so the card's sequence isn't optional.
tech: Used within the card's framing, as a critic of work the pupil has already produced, an approved AI tool in your setting can supply the external challenge that self-monitoring needs. The moment it starts drafting, planning or fixing on the pupil's behalf, though, it's the tool doing the regulating, and a pupil who always has the answer handed to them ends up needing the tool. Scaffold the regulation, then fade the scaffold, because the goal here, as everywhere in this strand, is a learner who no longer needs the tool.
pages.wider: Willingham's memory-as-residue-of-thought principle does the heavy lifting here, because whatever the pupil doesn't think about, the pupil doesn't learn, whoever or whatever did the thinking instead.
